title: Human Neuroimaging with MRI: A Primer
text:
Course Overview
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a primary scientific tool for measuring living human brain structure and function. This course bridges the gap between physics and application, teaching students how to generate anatomical images (sMRI and dMRI), measure quantitative tissue properties (qMRI), and assess brain activity (fMRI).

title: Human Neuroimaging with MRI: A Primer
text:
Who Should Take This Course?
We welcome students from engineering, neuroscience, and psychology backgrounds. The material is designed to help you transition into using MRI for your own research or to provide the technical literacy needed to critically evaluate scientific literature and collaborate effectively.

title: Human Neuroimaging with MRI: A Primer
text:
Instructional Approach
This course is designed around active, live interaction. While we provide Panopto recordings for occasional, unavoidable absences, the core value of the course lies in our synchronous discussions of research papers and collaborative homework reviews. We expect regular attendance to ensure a high-level dialogue that benefits the entire cohort.

title: Human Neuroimaging with MRI: A Primer
text:
Course topics
Review the menu at the left for an overview of the topics covered in the course. The different parts are collapsible, so you should be able to leaf through the coverage.

title: 1  MRI System
text:
1.1 MRI System: Multiple Rooms and Components
An MRI scanner is really a system, made up of many different sections. The hardware includes the main magnet, equipment for creating magnetic field gradients, radio frequency (RF) coils, power amplifiers, control electronics, and computers.
All these different components must communicate with one another, and their signals must be both accurate and synchronized. When you purchase an MRI scanner, you are really purchasing a system that spans several groups of instruments in different rooms.
Functional neuroimaging, one application of MRI, further requires systems that manage behavioral experiments. These systems are usually supplied by the research laboratory or specialized vendors. These present stimuli, record responses, and often monitor physiology such as respiration and heart rate. The timing of these systems must also be synchronized with the MR acquisition.
Let’s take a tour of the different parts of the system you would see at Stanford’s Center for Cognitive and Neurobiological Imaging (CNI).

text: Figure 1.1: Schematic of the multi-room MRI system (Huettel et al., Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging, 2e, Fig. 2.2).

title: 1  MRI System
text:
1.2 Control room






Figure 1.2: The control room for Stanford’s Center for Cognitive and Neurobiological Imaging (CNI).



Experimenters operate the scanner and monitor the subject from the control room. The primary operator console communicates with the scanner-control computer and displays the current scan, system status, and safety information.
Secondary computers are commonly used for stimulus presentation and response recording. Academic imaging centers usually provide interfaces for external laptops to control in-bore displays, sound systems, and button boxes. Supporting reliable connections for many research groups is an important operational requirement.






Figure 1.3: View of the control room window.



This view shows the scanner console and equipment used to connect button boxes, stimulus displays, and other devices in the scanner room. The shielded viewing window lets the operator observe the subject while preserving the room’s RF shielding.

title: 1  MRI System
text:
1.3 Scanner Room






Figure 1.4: Subject being positioned in the MR scanner.



The main magnet - big iron! - is in the scanner room. The magnet has a large bore where the patient table enters. Here, a subject is preparing to slide into the bore. He is adjusting a mirror that reflects an image from a display at the far end of the magnet. Even without a display, a mirror is often desirable so that the subject can see out of the bore to reduce claustrophobia.
The cable he is holding leads to a squeeze bulb, which gives the subject a direct way to alert the operator or stop the scan if needed.

title: 1  MRI System
text:
1.4 Radio frequency (RF) Shielding






Figure 1.5: Copper panels form the RF-shielded enclosure of the scanner room.



The scanner room has several forms of shielding for magnetic and radiofrequency fields.
The primary purpose of the shielding is to prevent unwanted radiofrequency (RF) signals from entering the scanner room. External broadcasts near the proton resonance frequency — about 127.7 MHz at 3 T — can contaminate the very weak MR signal received from the body.
The walls, ceiling, floor, door, and viewing window form a continuous conducting enclosure, usually made with copper or aluminum. Electrical cables pass through filtered penetration panels; nonconductive connections can use waveguides designed to block RF transmission. Together these components make a Faraday cage.
The Faraday cage attenuates RF electromagnetic waves in both directions, but it has essentially no effect on the static main field \(B_0\).
The magnet’s own active or passive magnetic shielding limits the fringe field (the region outside the scanner where the static field remains appreciable). This field typically extends several meters, and scanner facilities mark locations where it reaches 5 gauss (0.5 mT) or another locally specified safety threshold.

title: 1  MRI System
text:
1.5 Machine Room
The machine room sits adjacent to the scanner room. It contains equipment that has to be near the magnet but is kept outside the scanner room because of space, heat, noise, and electromagnetic-interference constraints.

Machine roomGradient amplifiersPeoplePatch panel and waveguides








Figure 1.6: The machine room, showing gradient amplifiers and support infrastructure.











Figure 1.7: Close-up of the gradient amplifier electronics rack.











Figure 1.8: The machine room: Adam Kerr and Michael Perry at the patch panel connecting the machine room to the scanner room.











Figure 1.9: Waveguides and patch panel on the scanner room wall.






These panel tabs show several views of the CNI machine room.
The machine room houses critical supporting infrastructure, including gradient and RF amplifiers, power supplies, cooling hardware, and penetration panels. Many cables and pipes pass between the machine room and the scanner room. Conductive cables use filtered feedthroughs, while waveguides provide RF-safe paths for appropriate connections.
The last two tabs show the patch panel, where those connections are made, and the people who keep this infrastructure operating.

title: 1  MRI System
text:
1.6 Chilled Water Cooling






Figure 1.10: Chilled water cooling system in the machine room.



A chilled-water loop removes heat from components that dissipate substantial power during scanning. Rapidly switched currents heat the gradient coils, and the gradient and RF power amplifiers also generate considerable heat.
The machine room also holds the helium compressor, which supplies high-pressure helium gas to the cryocooler’s cold head, mounted on the magnet. The compressor is another significant heat source, and it runs continuously — the magnet’s cooling does not pause between scans. Robust thermal management prevents scanner shutdowns and component degradation.

title: 1  MRI System
text:
1.7 Liquid Helium

Multiple dewarsDewar closeup








Figure 1.11: Liquid helium Dewars stored in the hallway outside the scanner room.











Figure 1.12: Close-up of a liquid helium Dewar with MRI KeepCOLD Services label.






Liquid helium is essential for the operation of many superconducting MRI scanners. It is delivered in large dewars.
Dewars are large, double-walled cryogenic vessels used to transport and store liquid helium. A high vacuum between the inner and outer walls, together with radiation shielding, greatly reduces heat transfer. Their walls are designed to be mechanically strong while limiting heat flow to the liquid.
Liquid helium keeps the magnet windings near 4.2 K (\(-269^\circ\text{C}\)), below the critical temperature of niobium-titanium (NbTi) wire. Many modern MRI scanners use a cryocooler, whose cold head is mounted on the magnet, to recondense helium vapor. This minimizes boil-off and reduces the need for cryogen refills.

title: 1  MRI System
text:
1.8 MRI Vendors






Figure 1.13: The three major vendors of human MRI systems: GE, Siemens, and Philips.



GE HealthCare, Siemens Healthineers, and Philips are longstanding major suppliers of human MRI systems. The underlying physics is the same across platforms, but software interfaces, gradient hardware, pulse-sequence implementations, and image-reconstruction algorithms differ. These differences can introduce vendor-specific variation, so multisite studies often require explicit harmonization before data are pooled. Bruker is a major supplier of small-bore preclinical systems; other manufacturers also serve the clinical and research markets.

title: 2  Main Field and Gradient Coils
text:
2.1 Main Field and Gradient-Coil Overview
Electricity and magnetism are inseparable in an MRI scanner: electric currents generate the main, gradient, and RF magnetic fields. You will hear about these signals and their measurement units whenever you read about MR experiments. Several important units of electricity and magnetism are named after the three scientists in the slide: Oersted (Oe), Tesla (T), and Gauss (G).
The connection between electricity and magnetism was first demonstrated by the Danish physicist Hans Christian Ørsted in 1820, when he showed that a current-carrying wire deflected a compass needle placed beneath it — the experiment sketched at the lower right of the slide. Gauss developed mathematical foundations for describing magnetic fields, and Tesla applied these principles in practical electromagnetic devices.
In MRI, the main field \(B_0\) is normally specified in tesla. For scale, Earth’s magnetic field is about 0.5 gauss, and a refrigerator magnet is roughly 200 gauss. Most clinical MRI systems operate at 1.5 or 3 tesla; higher-field human systems, such as 7 T and 9.4 T, are used primarily for research, although 7 T has limited clinical use.

text: Figure 2.1: Magnetic-field units and the scientists whose names they bear: Ørsted, Tesla, and Gauss.

title: 2  Main Field and Gradient Coils
text:
2.2 Magnetic Field Units






Figure 2.2: Magnetic-field unit conversions for magnetic field strength (\(H\)) and magnetic flux density (\(B\)).



Two related magnetic field quantities describe magnetic effects:

H (magnetic field strength): measured in amperes per meter (A/m)
B (magnetic flux density): measured in tesla (T)

In free space, these quantities are related by:
\[B = \mu_0 H\]
where the permeability of free space is \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\) T·m/A. Look at the units. You can see that the constant converts the units of H into the units of B.
Within magnetic materials, magnetization also contributes to \(B\), so the scalar relating them depends on the material.
MRI conventionally reports \(B_0\) in tesla; \(1\ \text{T} = 10{,}000\ \text{G}\).
crumbs: 2  Main Field and Gradient Coils

title: 2  Main Field and Gradient Coils
text:
2.3 Generating the Static Magnetic Field (\(B_0\))

2.3.1 The Helmholtz Pair

Schematic Helmholtz pairReal Helmholtz pair








Figure 2.3: Helmholtz pair: two current-carrying loops separated by one radius, producing a relatively uniform field at their midpoint.











Figure 2.4: A real Helmholtz pair: two coils of equal radius, separated by one radius.






A simple way to create a magnetic field is to run current through a pair of wires. The simplest example is the Helmholtz pair, which uses two loops carrying current in the same direction, separated by a distance equal to their radius. This geometry produces a relatively uniform field in the region between the coils. A pair can be made large enough to surround a human head, but this simple geometry cannot achieve the stringent homogeneity required throughout an MRI imaging volume.


2.3.2 The Solenoid Design






Figure 2.5: A solenoid: many closely spaced turns of wire arranged around a cylindrical form (Huettel et al., Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging, 2e).



To produce a more uniform field over a large volume, an MRI main magnet uses multiple, carefully positioned coaxial windings. Starting with two, and then going to many, is something you will see again and again in engineering design and practice.
The number, placement, and current of the loops (usually called **windings*) determine the magnetic field strength and its uniformity (homogeneity). Adding windings or increasing current through the windings increases the field; in an MRI magnet, the winding geometry is optimized to make \(B_0\) highly uniform throughout the imaging volume.
crumbs: 2  Main Field and Gradient Coils

title: 2  Main Field and Gradient Coils
text:
2.4 Superconducting Magnets






Figure 2.6: Superconducting magnet winding: niobium-titanium (NbTi) wire wound onto a cylindrical former.



If an MR magnet windings were made with conventional resistive conductor, such as copper, maintaining an MRI-strength magnetic field would dissipate enormous power. MR scanners are only practical because superconducting technology permits persistent current to flow with negligible resistance. The key is to achieving this state is that the conductor must remain below its critical temperature, magnetic-field, and current limits.
The superconducting wire in MRI magnets is commonly niobium-titanium (NbTi) wire. It is wound into multiple loops and kept below its critical temperature, typically near 4 Kelvin in a liquid helium cryostat. A superconducting switch closes the circuit after the magnet is ramped to field, allowing the current to circulate round and roun through the windings, with essentially no resistance and thus no loss. The cryogenic system requires power to maintain the low temperature, but it requires no power to run the massive current through the windings.






Figure 2.7: Cryocooler (cold head) operation: recondensing boiled-off helium to minimize consumption.



Liquid helium is the traditional primary cryogen. Thermal shields and vacuum insulation reduce the heat reaching the helium vessel; older magnet designs sometimes used liquid nitrogen as an additional, relatively inexpensive thermal shield.
Many modern superconducting MR systems use a cryocooler (cold head) to remove heat from the cryostat. In a recondensing system, the cold head condenses helium vapor back into liquid, greatly reducing helium loss and the need for refills. The cryocooler operates with a separate, closed helium-gas cycle that alternately compresses and expands the gas to create a cold stage near 4 K.
crumbs: 2  Main Field and Gradient Coils

title: 2  Main Field and Gradient Coils
text:
2.5 Gradient Coils
The main magnet’s job is to make \(B_0\) as uniform as possible. The gradient coils do the opposite: they deliberately add a small, controlled, spatially varying field on top of \(B_0\), so that the resonant frequency depends on position. This spatial encoding, together with RF excitation, signal reception, and image reconstruction, makes MRI possible; the encoding is developed fully in the image-formation part of the book.

2.5.1 The Maxwell Pair: a Z Gradient






Figure 2.8: The Maxwell pair: two coils carrying current in opposite directions, producing a field that varies linearly along the z-axis when superimposed on \(B_0\).



Unlike the Helmholtz pair, the two coils of a Maxwell pair carry current in opposite directions. Their fields cancel at isocenter and change approximately linearly near the center. When this field is added to the main field, the local axial field is approximately \(B_z(z) = B_0 + G_z z\), where \(G_z\) is the z-gradient amplitude in T/m. This z-gradient makes the field strength depend on position along the bore.


2.5.2 Three Orthogonal Gradient Fields






Figure 2.9: The three MR gradient coils (X, Y, Z) shown in their physical arrangement inside the scanner bore.



MRI requires three independently controlled gradient fields to encode position in all three dimensions. The z-gradient is often produced by a Maxwell-like pair of loops; the x- and y-gradients use saddle-shaped windings around the bore. Each produces a field that varies approximately linearly along its named axis, allowing the scanner to select and encode spatial locations.
All three gradient coils, along with the RF body coil, are nested concentrically inside the bore of the main magnet — the arrangement shown in Figure 2.9.






Saddle-shaped windings



In a simplified transverse-gradient design, saddle-shaped conductors lie on the cylindrical surface of the bore. Their straight sections run lengthwise along the cylinder and are joined by curved end sections, so the pattern resembles a saddle on a horse. Two symmetric saddle pairs can produce the desired transverse gradient while cancelling unwanted uniform and higher-order fields. Practical whole-body gradient coils use more complex distributed winding patterns, optimized for linearity, efficiency, Lorentz forces, heating, and peripheral-nerve-stimulation limits.
The conductors are manufactured and positioned very precisely, then driven together as one gradient coil. They are not ordinarily calibrated as independent saddles. Instead, scanner calibration measures the behavior of the complete gradient system — its amplitude, axis alignment, cross-axis coupling, timing, and eddy currents — and adjusts amplifier gains and pre-emphasis to correct residual errors.








Figure 2.10: A cutaway view of the scanner, showing how the components nest: the main magnet on the outside, the gradient coils inside it, the RF coil assembly nearest the patient, and the patient table.



Figure 2.10 puts the whole instrument together. Working outward from the subject: the RF transmit and receive hardware (Section 3.1), then the three gradient coils that encode position, then the superconducting main magnet that supplies \(B_0\). Each layer of that diagram corresponds to a section of this part of the book.

title: 2  Main Field and Gradient Coils
text:
2.6 Shimming






Figure 2.11: Shimming insert used to improve field homogeneity.



For all of the high technology, some methods for adjusting the magnetic field are remarkably simple. This image shows a small ferromagnetic piece that can be positioned along a holder to make a local correction to \(B_0\). These passive shims reduce selected spatial variations in \(B_0\); scanners also use actively controlled shim coils for adjustable corrections. Neither method makes the field perfectly homogeneous or corrects all subject-induced susceptibility effects.

title: 3  Radiofrequency Coils
text:
3.1 RF Coils Overview
Radiofrequency (RF) coils serve two functions in an MRI system.
One coil can transmit and receive at different times. In most human MRI systems, however, the built-in body coil transmits and a separate coil array receives. Coil design strongly affects sensitivity, spatial coverage, and the speed of an acquisition. The coils are an extremely important part of MR instrumentation.

title: 3  Radiofrequency Coils
text:
Figure 3.1: RF coils transmit excitation and receive the MR signal.





A transmit coil produces the RF magnetic field that tips the nuclear spins.
A receive coil detects the weak voltage induced by the precessing transverse magnetization.

title: 3  Radiofrequency Coils
text:
3.2 Surface Coils






Figure 3.2: Surface-coil description: alternating current in the loop generates an oscillating magnetic field that can excite the spins (Huettel et al., Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging, 2e).



A surface coil is a conducting loop with capacitors that form a resonant circuit. Every real coil also has resistance and other sources of loss. The circuit is tuned to the Larmor frequency; we will return to that frequency when we discuss the free-induction-decay experiment.
Surface coils provide high local sensitivity but limited spatial coverage — they work best for structures close to the coil surface.






LC circuits



The loop behaves as an inductor: alternating current in the loop produces an oscillating \(B_1\) field. Capacitors tune the circuit to resonance and are also used to match the coil to the transmitter or receiver. Resistance represents unavoidable energy loss; it does not provide the impedance match.
The idealized behavior of capacitors and inductors can be compared as follows.








Feature
Capacitor
Inductor




Energy storage
Stores energy in an electric field
Stores energy in a magnetic field


Response to change
Opposes changes in voltage
Opposes changes in current


Ideal impedance
High at DC; decreases with AC frequency
Low at DC; increases with AC frequency


Phase relationship
Current leads voltage by 90°
Voltage leads current by 90°


Basic construction
Two conductive plates separated by a dielectric
A coil of wire, often wound around a core

title: 3  Radiofrequency Coils
section: 3.3 Volume Coils and the Birdcage Design
text:
3.3 Volume Coils and the Birdcage Design






Figure 3.3: Volume coil (birdcage): the LC circuit is repeated around the surface of a cylinder, producing more uniform spatial coverage but lower local sensitivity (Huettel et al., Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging, 2e).



A volume coil distributes conductors and capacitors around a cylinder to generate a relatively uniform \(B_1\) field over a large volume. The birdcage design — multiple conducting rungs connected by end rings — is the standard approach. Its elements form one coupled resonant structure, rather than independent receiver channels whose signals are simply added. The coil in Figure 3.3 excites the whole head at once, with far less variation across the volume than a surface coil.






Figure 3.4: The birdcage design is widely used for the body transmit coil, built into the main magnet bore.



The most important example is the body coil, which is built into the scanner. It is driven in its uniform, circularly polarized mode to provide RF excitation throughout the magnet bore.
At 3 T, and especially at 7 T and above, the RF wavelength in tissue and coupling between the coil and patient become important. These effects can make the transmit field non-uniform and increase SAR, motivating more complex, multi-transmit driving schemes.

title: 3  Radiofrequency Coils
text:
3.4 Phased-Array Coils






Figure 3.5: Phased-array coil: combines multiple independent surface coils to balance sensitivity and spatial coverage (Huettel et al., Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging, 2e).



A phased-array coil combines multiple small, independent surface-coil elements — each with its own receiver channel — arranged to cover a larger region. Unlike a volume coil, each element detects signal from its local neighborhood with high sensitivity. The elements are designed to be decoupled so that they do not substantially interfere with one another.
The signals are measured separately and combined computationally to produce an image. This arrangement provides broad coverage while retaining good local signal-to-noise ratio (SNR).






Figure 3.6: Phased-array head coils: comparing 12-channel and 32-channel configurations (Kaza et al., JMRI, 2011).



Phased-array coils enable parallel imaging (e.g., SENSE and GRAPPA), which uses the different spatial sensitivity profiles of the elements as additional encoding information. This permits faster acquisitions; we will describe the idea later. More channels can improve SNR and parallel-imaging performance, but only with appropriate element design and greater hardware complexity.

title: 3  Radiofrequency Coils
text:
3.5 Head Coils in Practice

Multiple parallel-receive head coilsClose-up: 64-channel coil (Stockmann/MGH)








Figure 3.7: High-channel-count head coils developed at the University of Minnesota for ultra-high-field imaging.











Figure 3.8: The 64-channel head coil project at Stanford: assembled by Kawin Setsompop’s group, Adam Kerr, and Jason Stockmann from MGH.






High-channel-count head coils are still largely hand-assembled, requiring careful placement, tuning, and decoupling of each element. The 64-channel coil shown here was assembled for the CNI in collaboration with Massachusetts General Hospital. Coil construction remains something of an art: small changes in one element can alter the tuning or coupling of its neighbors.

title: 3  Radiofrequency Coils
text:
3.6 Coil Design and Simulation

Software for head-coil designSimulation of the signal








Figure 3.9: COMSOL simulation of a birdcage coil: modeling the B1 field distribution inside a human head phantom.











Figure 3.10: Simulated sensitivity (B1 field strength) of a birdcage coil across a human head phantom.






Electromagnetic simulation tools such as COMSOL, CST Studio Suite, and Sim4Life model the transmit and receive RF fields inside the patient, as well as the electric field. They are used to estimate the specific absorption rate (SAR), the RF power absorbed per unit mass of tissue. These simulations are essential for safety evaluation, particularly at high field strengths where transmit-field inhomogeneity and local SAR become more significant.

title: 3  Radiofrequency Coils
text:
3.7 Commercial Coils






Figure 3.11: Nova Medical: a leading commercial manufacturer of high-performance phased-array RF coils for research MRI.



Many research sites use coils from specialized manufacturers rather than from the scanner vendor. Nova Medical is a widely used supplier of high-channel-count head coils for Siemens, GE, and Philips scanners. Other specialized manufacturers include RAPID Biomedical, ScanMed, and PulseTeq.

title: 3  Radiofrequency Coils
text:
3.8 Image Quality Across Coil Types






Figure 3.12: Comparison of brain images acquired with surface, volume (birdcage), and phased-array RF coils (Huettel et al., Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging, 2e).



Surface coils provide high SNR near the coil, but their sensitivity falls rapidly with distance. Volume coils provide more uniform coverage across the whole brain, usually with lower receive sensitivity. Phased-array coils combine the local sensitivity of many elements to provide broad coverage and high SNR. Their raw sensitivity is still spatially non-uniform, so image reconstruction often includes a coil-combination or intensity-correction step. This balance makes phased arrays the standard receive coils for modern neuroimaging.

title: 4  MRI Safety
text:
4.1 Safety Considerations Overview
This chapter covers five topics:

title: 4  MRI Safety
text:
Static-field projectile and torque hazards, including screening and access control
Gradient-field peripheral nerve stimulation and acoustic noise
RF heating and burn prevention
Magnet quenches and cryogen safety
Real-world accidents

title: 4  MRI Safety
text:
4.2 Main Magnetic Field (\(B_0\)): General Properties






Figure 4.1: B0 field properties relevant to safety: field strengths used clinically, field uniformity specifications, and field stability.



Human body-size MR scanners are most commonly operated at 1.5 T and 3 T, with a smaller number at 7 T and very few at 9.4 T or above. Field homogeneity and stability are scanner-specific specifications, normally reported in ppm over a stated diameter spherical volume. MR physicists also use small-bore systems at much higher field strengths for animal imaging and chemical spectroscopy; the smaller imaging volume makes high field and stringent homogeneity more tractable.

title: 4  MRI Safety
text:
4.3 Ferromagnetic Objects and Projectile Hazards






Figure 4.2: Ferromagnetic objects near MR scanners become dangerous projectiles: examples include a chair, oxygen canister, and power supply drawn into the bore.



The persistent static field creates two related hazards: the projectile effect, in which a ferromagnetic object is pulled toward the bore, and torque, which tends to rotate an elongated ferromagnetic object into alignment with the field. Common hazardous objects include oxygen canisters, IV poles, tools, and scissors, as well as many iron- or steel-containing items. The magnet remains at field between scans and overnight, so screening and control of people and objects entering the MR environment are essential.
When operating conditions and screening procedures are followed, temporary exposure to the MR environment has no known health hazard. The static field can nevertheless move or torque unsafe objects and implants. Subjects moving quickly through a strong field may report transient dizziness, a metallic taste, or visual flickers. Rapidly switching gradient fields can induce peripheral nerve stimulation and produce acoustic noise that requires hearing protection. RF energy can heat tissue and conductive materials; burn prevention requires attention to patient positioning, cables, conductive loops, implants, and the sequence-specific SAR limits (Section 3.1).

title: 4  MRI Safety
text:
4.4 Screening, Labels, and Patient Protection
Every patient, visitor, and item entering the MR environment must be screened according to site policy. Implants and devices must be positively identified and their MR Safe, MR Conditional, or MR Unsafe status verified. An MR Conditional device may be used only under its specified field strength, spatial-gradient, RF, and operating conditions. Padding, cable management, avoidance of skin-to-skin conductive loops, and appropriate hearing protection reduce avoidable RF-burn and acoustic-injury risks.

title: 4  MRI Safety
text:
4.5 Real-World Safety Incidents

4.5.1 Local Example: Mountain View






Figure 4.3: News report of a projectile accident at a Mountain View MRI facility.



This local report illustrates that projectile incidents can occur whenever screening, access control, or object control fails. Reference: KTVU report



4.5.2 Redwood City (Kaiser) Example






Figure 4.4: Video still from a Kaiser Redwood City MRI safety incident.

title: 4  MRI Safety
text:
4.6 Magnet Quench






Figure 4.5: Sequence of photographs showing a superconducting magnet quench event at a manufacturing facility.



A superconducting magnet operating in persistent mode can maintain current without continuous electrical power to its windings, but its cryogenic support system still requires power. A quench is a sudden loss of superconductivity: resistance develops, stored magnetic energy is converted to heat, and the resulting heating can drive a rapid transition through the winding. Cooling failure is one possible trigger; mechanical, electrical, or other disturbances can also initiate a quench. In helium-bath systems, the deposited heat vaporizes liquid helium rapidly and can produce a large volume of cold gas.
Helium is inert, but a quench can create cold-injury, pressure, oxygen-displacement, and visibility hazards. The exhaust and emergency response arrangements depend on the magnet and installation; personnel must follow the site’s MR-safety and quench procedures rather than assume that a release is harmless.
Here are links to many YouTube videos of quenches, and tutorials about an MR Quench.

title: 4  MRI Safety
text:
4.7 Recent Accident (Korea)

title: 4  MRI Safety
text:
4.8 The Size of Magnetic Forces
The forces involved near a high-field magnet are difficult to appreciate without direct experience. The displacement force on a ferromagnetic object depends on the static field and its spatial gradient; torque also depends on the object’s shape and orientation. These effects can change rapidly in the fringe field, so an object that seems manageable at one location can become hazardous nearer the bore. Even experienced MRI staff must maintain strict protocols to prevent accidents.






Figure 4.7: Hitachi 0.7T open-platform surgical MRI scanner — an alternative geometry that reduces some access constraints.



Many open-platform scanners use a vertical field geometry with a gap between the upper and lower magnet assemblies. Their lower field strength often reduces the available SNR under otherwise comparable conditions, but the open geometry can improve surgical access and patient tolerance. The appropriate scanner depends on the clinical task and the required image quality.
Even relatively low-field systems can present substantial projectile and torque hazards. Safety precautions depend on the scanner’s field map and the object’s material, shape, and location—not on nominal field strength alone.

title: 5  MR Signal Fundamentals
text:
5.1 Fundamental MR measurements
In this section we introduce a fundamental magnetic-resonance experiment, the free induction decay (FID). To understand this experiment, we only need to consider two parts of the instrument: the main magnetic field and the radiofrequency coils. We will explain the use of imaging gradients in later chapters.
But I want you to see where we are headed. So before I describe the FID, let’s have a look at the console, where a user sits down to set up the parameters for an MRI experiment. We are going to build up our understanding from the very simple FID experiment to a system that can make an extraordinary range of measurements.

title: 5  MR Signal Fundamentals
text: Figure 5.1: The main elements we control in the MR instrument (McRobbie et al., MRI: From Picture to Proton, 2e, Fig. 9.1).

Figure 5.3: User’s console: Adjusts pulse sequence parameters — step 2.











Figure 5.4: User’s console: Adjusts pulse sequence parameters — step 3.






At the console, the user defines a program that controls the RF signal and the imaging gradients. The orchestration of these signals—their amplitudes and timing—is called pulse-sequence programming. The three tabs show screenshots with the various parameters we set to control the pulse sequence.

title: 5  MR Signal Fundamentals
text:
5.3 MR pulse sequences






Figure 5.5: MR pulse sequences.



This diagram shows a conventional way to represent a pulse sequence. It represents the controls for a classic sequence called spin echo, which we will study later. For now, notice that the horizontal axis represents time, increasing from left to right. Each line shows how we control one sequence component, such as a gradient or the RF excitation.
By choosing different parameter timings, we can acquire signals with different sensitivities to tissue properties. The pulse sequence is adjusted to highlight certain differences between tissues and diminish others.
The MR images that we produce are not at all what you see if you look at the brain with your eye. MR images are reconstructed from electrical signals detected after RF excitation. Those signals depend on tissue properties, allowing MRI to make otherwise invisible tissue differences visible.

title: 5  MR Signal Fundamentals
text:
5.4 MR quantities (weighted)






Figure 5.6: MR quantities (weighted).



This slide shows three images from a similar slice of a brain, obtained using three different pulse sequences. The three sequences have different sensitivity to tissue properties.

title: 5  MR Signal Fundamentals
text:
5.5 MR pulse sequence parameter choices






Figure 5.7: MR pulse sequence parameter choices.



Altering the values of the parameters produces signals with different sensitivities to physical properties of the sample.
In this image array, the authors used a spin-echo sequence while varying the timing parameters (TE and TR). This is often a useful way to understand a system.
This experiment demonstrates that the MR instrument is quite flexible. The same instrument can be programmed to measure different aspects of the tissue under study.






Note



Looking ahead: In Chapter 9b, we’ll explore specific pulse sequence implementations like spin echo and learn how timing parameters (TE/TR) create different tissue weightings.

title: 5  MR Signal Fundamentals
text:
5.6 To the future – and beyond






Figure 5.8: To the future – and beyond.



Much is known about the relationship between the sequence, its parameters, and the underlying tissue. But this field is certainly not fully worked out. New discoveries continue to be made and people invent new ideas about pulse sequences that enable us to measure new things. One of the main topics of this course, measuring functional signals from the brain, was only invented thirty years ago. Many new ideas continue to emerge.
Those ideas will be built upon the foundations that we do understand today. The most fundamental observation is the free induction decay (FID) experiment. We introduce this experiment in the next section.

title: 5  MR Signal Fundamentals
text:
5.7 Free induction decay



The substrateThe equipmentThe signal








Figure 5.9: The substrate, in this case a beaker of water, is placed in a uniform magnetic field.











Figure 5.10: We apply an RF pulse to the substrate using an RF coil. The pulse is an oscillating signal at a chosen frequency. After the RF excitation, the same coil detects a voltage induced by the substrate.











Figure 5.11: The measured voltage oscillates. The response starts with a relatively high amplitude and decays over time.






We are now ready for the free induction decay measurement, the simplest MR signal experiment. The idea of the experiment is built up in the series of images in this panel.
We place a beaker of water, in this example, inside a uniform magnetic field. We then apply an RF pulse at a chosen frequency. After the pulse, the coil detects a voltage induced by the sample. That’s it.
Remember—at this point in our understanding, we are not measuring an image. We are measuring one time-varying voltage signal from a beaker of water. It will be a little while before we get to the topic of how we might form an image. The following material is all about measurements from a single volume.

title: 5  MR Signal Fundamentals
section: 5.8 The FID signal depends on RF-pulse duration
text:
5.8 The FID signal depends on RF-pulse duration
The three images in this panel show an interesting—and surprising—aspect of the FID experiment. We hold the other experimental settings fixed and vary the duration of the RF excitation pulse. We will explain this observation after developing a model of the magnetic-resonance experiment.

ShortMediumLong








Figure 5.12: The FID signal depends on RF-pulse duration — step 1.











Figure 5.13: The middle duration RF pulse.











Figure 5.14: The longest duration RF pulse.






As we increase the duration of the RF excitation pulse, the signal initially increases. But as the RF pulse gets longer, the signal decreases and can nearly disappear. Why?

title: 6  The MR Macroscopic Model
text:
6.1 From the FID experiment to a model
In the free-induction-decay (FID) experiment, we apply an RF pulse to a sample of water and record an oscillating voltage that decays over time. We also saw that changing the duration of the RF pulse first increases and then decreases the initial signal. This chapter develops a macroscopic model that explains both observations.
The model has four steps: the main field, \(B_0\), creates an equilibrium net magnetization; the RF field, \(B_1\), tips it; the resulting transverse magnetization precesses; and that precession induces the voltage recorded by a receiver coil.

title: 6  The MR Macroscopic Model
section: 6.2 Hydrogen nuclei are the source of the MR signal
text:
6.2 Hydrogen nuclei are the source of the MR signal






Figure 6.1: Source of the MR signal: Hydrogen nuclei (spins, protons) (after Huettel et al., Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging, 2e, Fig. 3.2).



The FID arises from hydrogen nuclei, primarily those in water. Each hydrogen nucleus is a proton with spin and an associated magnetic moment. Spin is a quantum-mechanical property, but a magnetic-dipole model provides useful intuition for the bulk behavior measured in MRI.

title: 6  The MR Macroscopic Model
section: 6.3 The main field establishes equilibrium magnetization
text:
6.3 The main field establishes equilibrium magnetization
In the absence of an applied field, an ensemble of proton magnetic moments has no preferred direction, so its net magnetization is zero. Placing the sample in the main magnetic field, \(B_0\), establishes a preferred longitudinal direction.






Figure 6.2: A simplified classical depiction of a proton magnetic moment precessing about the main field, \(B_0\).



In the classical picture, a magnetic moment precesses about \(B_0\), like a spinning top in Earth’s gravitational field. This picture is an analogy, not a literal spinning charged sphere.






Figure 6.3: A simplified classical depiction of a magnetic moment precessing about \(B_0\).



For a single spin-\(1/2\) proton, a measurement of the spin component along \(B_0\) has one of two values, conventionally called parallel and antiparallel. At thermal equilibrium, there is a small excess in the lower-energy, parallel state. That excess produces the longitudinal equilibrium magnetization, \(M_0\).






Figure 6.4: A schematic ensemble of proton magnetic moments without an applied field (left) and in the main field, \(B_0\) (right). The small population excess parallel to \(B_0\) produces a net magnetization, \(M_0\).



We summarize the ensemble by its net magnetization, the vector sum of its individual magnetic moments. At equilibrium, the net magnetization is \(\mathbf{M}=M_0\hat{\mathbf z}\): it points along \(B_0\), which defines the \(z\)-axis. The transverse components cancel because their phases are distributed around the axis.






Figure 6.5: The net magnetization is the sum of the spins (after Huettel et al., Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging, 2e, Fig. 3.7).

title: 6  The MR Macroscopic Model
section: 6.4 An RF pulse creates transverse magnetization
text:
6.4 An RF pulse creates transverse magnetization


Video
The \(B_1\) field applies a torque that tips \(\mathbf{M}\) away from the \(z\)-axis, creating transverse magnetization.


The transmit coil produces an RF magnetic field, \(B_1\), that is transverse to \(B_0\) and oscillates near the Larmor frequency. In the usual idealized description, this field applies a torque that tips \(\mathbf{M}\) away from the \(z\)-axis, creating transverse magnetization, \(M_{xy}\).

title: 6  The MR Macroscopic Model
text:
6.5 Rotating and laboratory frames






Figure 6.6: The RF field, \(B_1\), in the rotating-frame and laboratory-frame views (Huettel et al., Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging, 2e).



The rotating-frame and laboratory-frame descriptions show the same excitation from two useful viewpoints. In the laboratory frame, the transverse magnetization precesses rapidly about \(B_0\); in a frame rotating at the Larmor frequency, a resonant \(B_1\) field can appear nearly stationary.

title: 6  The MR Macroscopic Model
text:
6.6 Precession induces the receiver-coil voltage



Video


Figure 6.7: The transverse net magnetization precesses around the \(z\)-axis.



After excitation, \(M_{xy}\) precesses about the main field, \(B_0\). At equilibrium, the magnetization has no transverse component, so there is no corresponding oscillating voltage induced in the receiver coil.

6.6.1 Measuring the precessing net magnetization


Video
The precessing net magnetization induces a voltage in a receiver coil (shown here as the copper coil).


As the transverse net magnetization precesses, the magnetic flux through the receiver coil changes. By Faraday’s law, the changing flux induces a voltage whose sign and magnitude vary over time. The receiver records this voltage as the MR signal. The transmit and receiver coils can be the same physical coil or separate coils.


6.6.2 Transverse magnetization and the measured voltage






Figure 6.8: As transverse net magnetization rotates, the changing flux through the receiver coil induces a voltage (Huettel et al., Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging, 2e, Fig. 3.16).



Phase coherence produces a nonzero transverse magnetization, \(M_{xy}\). That rotating magnetization induces the time-varying voltage in the receiver coil. The receiver directly measures this voltage, whose causes must be interpreted to understand the MR signal.

title: 6  The MR Macroscopic Model
section: 6.7 Flip angle explains the effect of RF-pulse duration
text:
6.7 Flip angle explains the effect of RF-pulse duration






Figure 6.9: The FID signal depends on RF-pulse duration.



The amount by which an RF pulse tips \(\mathbf{M}\) is its flip angle, \(\alpha\). For an ideal resonant hard pulse, the flip angle increases with both the \(B_1\) amplitude and pulse duration. The initial transverse magnitude is proportional to \(M_0\sin\alpha\).
As \(\alpha\) increases from \(0^\circ\) to \(90^\circ\), the transverse magnetization and the initial FID voltage increase. At \(90^\circ\), all of \(\mathbf{M}\) is transverse and the magnitude is maximal. As the pulse continues toward \(180^\circ\), the transverse magnitude falls to zero; beyond \(180^\circ\), it returns with the opposite phase. This explains the pattern observed in the FID experiment.

title: 6  The MR Macroscopic Model
text:
6.8 Relaxation makes the FID decay






Figure 6.10: The FID signal: longitudinal recovery and transverse decay (Huettel et al., Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging, 2e, Fig. 3.5).



After an RF excitation pulse, the magnetization is displaced from equilibrium. Relaxation returns it toward equilibrium. The physical processes responsible for longitudinal recovery along the \(z\)-axis and transverse decay in the \(x\)-\(y\) plane differ. The next two chapters develop these processes as \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) relaxation.
For a deeper discussion of the quantum-mechanical representations used to draw individual NMR spins, see Drawing single NMR spins.

title: 7  T1 Relaxation
text:
7.1 Two components of net magnetization
The net magnetization vector can be separated into two components: its projection onto the \(z\)-axis, which we call the longitudinal component \(M_z\), and its projection onto the \(x\)-\(y\) plane, the transverse component \(M_{xy}\).
As we saw in the previous chapter, the transverse component precesses around the \(z\)-axis and induces a voltage in the receive coil. The coil does not directly detect \(M_z\). So what determines the longitudinal component, and how can we measure it indirectly?
The two components belong to the same net magnetization, but they change for different physical reasons. This is what makes MRI versatile: one instrument can be sensitive to different properties of the tissue.

title: 7  T1 Relaxation
text: Figure 7.1: The net magnetization has two components.

title: 7  T1 Relaxation
text:
7.2 Parallel and anti-parallel states






Figure 7.2: The longitudinal component: High- and low-stability states (Huettel et al., Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging, 2e, Fig. 3.6).



A proton’s spin component along \(B_0\) has two possible states: parallel and anti-parallel. At thermal equilibrium, slightly more protons occupy the lower-energy, parallel state. A loose metaphor to understand this difference is shown in Figure 7.2. The image shows two bars in a gravitational field, one that is hanging low and is in a low-energy state. It will stay that way unless a strong breeze comes along to move it.
The other bar is upright in a precarious state that is higher energy and less stable—even a weak breeze might cause it to fall over, dropping into the low-energy state.
The metaphor is useful, but it has limits. Protons are not tiny bars, and the net magnetization can point in intermediate directions in the vector description, especially after RF excitation. Here, “parallel” and “anti-parallel” refer specifically to the two possible outcomes for the spin component along \(B_0\).

title: 7  T1 Relaxation
section: 7.3 An RF pulse changes spins between the two states
text:
7.3 An RF pulse changes spins between the two states






Figure 7.3: Energy from an RF pulse changes spins between the two stable binary states (Huettel et al., Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging, 2e, Fig. 3.9).



The longitudinal net magnetization is proportional to the difference between the populations of the two states. An RF pulse can alter this population difference by driving transitions between the two states. The energy required for those transitions is determined by the separation between the two energy levels.

title: 7  T1 Relaxation
text:
7.4 Spin transition and quantum energy






Figure 7.4: Spin Transition and Quantum Energy (Huettel et al., Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging, 2e, Fig. 3.8).



For proton spins the energy separation between the parallel and anti-parallel states increases linearly with the main field, \(B_0\). This separation is called the Zeeman splitting.
An RF field at the resonant frequency can drive transitions between the two states. In the photon picture, the energy of one RF quantum is proportional to the frequency, with Planck’s constant as the constant of proportionality.
\[
\Delta E = h f_L.
\]

title: 7  T1 Relaxation
section: 7.5 The frequency depends on the \(B_0\) field
text:
7.5 The frequency depends on the \(B_0\) field






Figure 7.5: The Larmor frequency depends on the \(B_0\) field: \(f_L = \gamma B_0\), so the resonant frequency is 127.4 MHz at 3 T.



Putting these two facts together, we see that a higher \(B_0\) requires a higher resonant frequency, \(f_L\).
The relationship between magnetic-field strength and resonant frequency is linear. This frequency is called the Larmor frequency, after Joseph Larmor. It is the frequency an RF pulse must have to affect protons in a particular \(B_0\) field.
The Larmor frequency is
\[
f_L = \gamma B_0,
\]
where \(\gamma\) is the gyromagnetic ratio (42.58 MHz/T for hydrogen). At 1.5 T we excite and receive near 64 MHz, at 3 T near 127 MHz, and at 7 T near 300 MHz—all in the radio band. Higher field strength means a larger energy gap between the two spin states, a larger equilibrium population difference, and—other factors being equal—generally a larger MR signal. This is one important reason for building higher-field scanners.

title: 7  T1 Relaxation
text:
7.6 Spin-lattice interactions







Figure 7.6: Water in the axonal cross-section.



When a spin transitions from the high-energy state (anti-parallel) to the low-energy state (parallel), it gives off some energy. The energy has to go somewhere, so it is transferred to the surrounding molecular environment—the lattice. This is why \(T_1\) relaxation is also called spin-lattice relaxation.
How quickly this transfer happens depends on the local molecular environment. This is what makes \(T_1\) useful: in tissues in and around the brain, values range from a few hundred milliseconds for fat to several seconds for free water.

title: 7  T1 Relaxation
text:
7.7 Hydration layer






Figure 7.7: Hydration layer.



How do these molecular interactions relate to MRI measurements? The panels show a cross-section through a single axon, with individual myelin wraps visible, and then a schematic of one myelin-membrane layer: a lipid bilayer surrounded by water molecules.
The MR properties of water change when it interacts with a membrane surface. The water immediately in contact with the membrane—the apparent hydration layer—has different relaxation behavior from water farther away. A model based on quantitative \(T_1\) and proton-density mapping can estimate the apparent fraction of water interacting with membrane surfaces, which we will call the apparent hydration-layer fraction (aHLF) (Mezer et al., 2013). This is an indirect, model-based estimate; in white matter, it is expected to be higher where membrane surface area and myelin are greater.

title: 7  T1 Relaxation
text:
7.8 Longitudinal net magnetization recovery (T1)






Figure 7.8: Longitudinal net magnetization recovery (T1).



Let’s zoom out from individual spins to a beaker containing many spins. Figure 7.8 shows the net magnetization at several points. It begins at equilibrium in the \(B_0\) field. A resonant RF pulse then tips it 90 degrees away from the \(z\)-axis, so that \(M_z=0\) immediately afterward. Over time, the longitudinal component recovers toward its equilibrium value,
\[
M_z(t) = M_0\left(1 - e^{-t/T_1}\right)
\]
This equation is for the 90° flip-angle case: it assumes that the longitudinal component starts at zero. The slide asks what would happen after a 180° flip angle, which starts the magnetization at \(-M_0\) instead. We take that up in the inversion recovery chapter (Figure 10.1), where the negative starting value is central to the measurement.

title: 7  T1 Relaxation
text:
7.10 Why \(T_1\) values differ






Figure 7.9: Longitudinal relaxation rate depends on your neighborhood: recovery curves for gray matter (T1 = 0.88 s) and white matter (T1 = 0.65 s) at 1.5 T.



The \(T_1\) time constant depends on the molecular environment around the spins, which differs between gray matter and white matter. These differences in tissue chemistry and structure can contribute to contrast among CSF, gray matter, and white matter; the brightness in an image also depends on the pulse sequence and readout timing.
Thus, \(T_1\) is a measurable MR parameter that indirectly reflects the local molecular environment rather than directly measuring a particular tissue constituent.

title: 7  T1 Relaxation
text:
7.11 Image contrast






Figure 7.10: Contrast: the difference between signals: the gray/white magnetization difference is largest around 0.8 s after the RF pulse.



An image maps reconstructed signal values to displayed intensities. Image contrast is the difference in intensity between nearby tissues. A signal level has little meaning in isolation; spatial differences in intensity make edges and tissue boundaries visible.

title: 7  T1 Relaxation
text:
7.12 Calculating the contrast
The two normalized recovery curves in Figure 7.9 start together at zero and end together at \(M_0\). In this equal-\(M_0\) simulation, the difference is therefore zero at both ends and largest somewhere in between. Figure 7.10 plots that difference,
\[
\Delta M = M_0\left(e^{-t/T_{1,G}} - e^{-t/T_{1,W}}\right)
\]
Here, \(G\) and \(W\) denote gray and white matter.
The contrast for this particular simulation peaks around 0.8 s after the RF pulse at 1.5 T. This is a useful result: it tells us when to read out the signal in this simple experiment. Waiting too long is as bad as not waiting long enough, because both tissues have then nearly recovered to the same value. Choosing acquisition timing to emphasize a contrast of interest is a central design problem for a pulse sequence.

title: 7  T1 Relaxation
section: 7.13 The T1-contrast: white is brighter than gray
text:
7.13 The T1-contrast: white is brighter than gray






Figure 7.11: The T1-contrast distinguishes gray and white matter.



Putting the two ideas together: a longer \(T_1\) means slower recovery and therefore less longitudinal magnetization at readout, when the other factors are held fixed. In this simplified example, white matter (short \(T_1\)) is bright, gray matter is darker, and CSF (the longest \(T_1\) of the three) is darkest. Actual image brightness is sequence- and acquisition-dependent, but \(T_1\)-weighted volumes are widely used to distinguish gray matter from white matter and to support estimates of cortical thickness, atrophy, and ventricular enlargement.

title: 7  T1 Relaxation
text:
7.14 Surface Interaction Rate (SIR)






Figure 7.12: Surface Interaction Rate (SIR); portraits of Bloch and Purcell (Huettel et al., Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging, 2e, Fig. 1.13).



Once we recognize that \(T_1\) depends on the local molecular environment, we can cautiously relate a measurement to properties of cells and molecules in the brain. This model-based reasoning—from MR parameters to tissue properties—is an important part of quantitative MRI. We do not merely report the values; we use them to test hypotheses about the underlying biochemistry.
The \(T_1\) of free water is long because there are no nearby large molecules to absorb the excess energy efficiently. Freely moving water molecules have relatively few effective ways to pass that energy to their surroundings. Near a membrane or other macromolecule, the interaction is stronger, so the energy transfer is more efficient and \(T_1\) becomes shorter. BPP theory explains why the \(T_1\) of bulk free water is about 4.3 s at room temperature and is approximately independent of \(B_0\) over the usual MRI field range (Bloembergen et al., 1948). Yes, you should be amazed.
The \(T_1\) values for brain tissue, which contains many large molecules and membranes, are much shorter than the value for free water (0.65–0.9 s for white and gray matter at 1.5 T). Much of the water in tissue is near a macromolecular surface. Interactions between water and those large molecules can make energy transfer to the surrounding environment more efficient, shortening \(T_1\). As a rough approximation, a voxel’s \(T_1\) reflects how water interacts with its molecular environment; it does not isolate exchange in a hydration layer. For this reason, when properly accounting for other instrumental factors we can hope to measure the surface interaction rate (SIR) from the \(T_1\) measurements (Mezer et al., 2013).





Bloembergen, N., Purcell, E. M., & Pound, R. V. (1948). Relaxation effects in nuclear magnetic resonance absorption. Physical Review, 73(7), 679–712. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.73.679


Mezer, A., Yeatman, J. D., Stikov, N., Kay, K. N., Cho, N.-J., Dougherty, R. F., Perry, M. L., Parvizi, J., Hua, L. H., Butts-Pauly, K., & Wandell, B. A. (2013). Quantifying the local tissue volume and composition in individual brains with magnetic resonance imaging. Nature Medicine, 19(12), 1667–1672.

title: 8  T2 Relaxation and Signal Contrast
text:
8.1 The net magnetization is summarized by two components
As in Figure 7.1, we separate the net magnetization into a component along the z-axis (longitudinal) and a component in the x-y plane (transverse). T1 describes how the longitudinal component returns to equilibrium after an RF pulse. T2, which is boxed in this slide, describes how the transverse component returns to equilibirum.
Like the longitudinal component, we describe the transverse component as a vector. But this vector is dynamically rotating in a plane. Thus, it has both a changing length (amplitude) and a changing direction. Remember from the prior chapters, this rotating vector is the only signal we measure in an MR experiment.
A receive coil sits at one position and senses only the projection of that vector onto its own axis (Figure 6.8). As the transverse magnetization precesses around the z-axis, the projection points first toward the coil (positive) and then away from it (negative). The measured signal oscillates at the Larmor frequency as the vector rotates. The amplitude of that oscillation decays over time. The time constant of the day of the transverse vector is T2.
crumbs: 8  T2 Relaxation and Signal Contrast

title: 8  T2 Relaxation and Signal Contrast
text: Figure 8.1: The net magnetization is summarized by two components.
crumbs: 8  T2 Relaxation and Signal Contrast

title: 8  T2 Relaxation and Signal Contrast
text:
8.2 Transverse relaxation: T2






Figure 8.2: Transverse relaxation: T2. The net transverse magnetization (red arrow, bottom row) is zero before excitation, large immediately after the RF pulse, and decays back to zero as the individual spins lose their common phase.



Before the RF pulse, the spins have no common transverse direction. This is true in field-free space, and it remains true after we place a head in the B0 field: B0 creates a preferred direction along z, but it creates no preferred direction in the x-y plane. The individual transverse components point every which way and cancel, so there is no net transverse magnetization and the coil measures nothing.
The RF pulse changes this. It tips the spins away from the z-axis and, just as important, it leaves them precessing together — in phase. Now the individual transverse components add rather than cancel, and we do measure a signal from the coherent transverse magnetization.
The sequence of events is summarized in Figure 8.2. The red arrow below the vectors of spins shows the net transverse magnetization over time. It starts out as a dot (zero length, no direction). After RF excitation the net is large and precessing around the z-axis. Then, as the individual spins lose their common phase — becoming incoherent — the net transverse magnetization shrinks back to zero, here over a couple of hundred milliseconds. The decay is exponential,
\[
M_{xy}(t) = M_0\,e^{-t/T_2}
\]
and T2 is its time constant.
crumbs: 8  T2 Relaxation and Signal Contrast

title: 8  T2 Relaxation and Signal Contrast
text:
8.3 The spin de-phasing



Video
Individual magnetic moments start aligned and progressively de-phase (become incoherent); the sum of the magnetic moments, and the resulting signal, decays as the individual spins diverge.


When the spins share a common phase, we say they are in phase, or coherent. The loss of that common phase is called de-phasing.
The video represents the de-phasing, but in a special way. Remember that the transverse magnetization is always precessing around the z-axis, far too quickly to display. So we imagine ourselves rotating around the z-axis at that same pace — the rotating frame. If we do not rotate around at the precession frequency, we say we are in the lab frame. In the rotating frame the common precession becomes invisible, and what remains visible is exactly what we care about: the individual moments fanning out relative to one another.

Transverse magnetization declines as the directions of the spins (their relative phases) diverge, becoming incoherent
The colored vectors on the left represent the individual magnetic moments (spins); they begin aligned and progressively spread apart
The blue arrow on the right is the sum of those moments — the net transverse magnetization — which shortens as the spins de-phase
The curve at the bottom shows how the amplitude of that sum decays over time

But do remember what this amplitude means. The signal in the coil swings back and forth, from positive to negative, as the transverse magnetization goes round and round the z-axis. The decaying curve is the envelope of that oscillation, not the oscillation itself. This decaying oscillation, measured after a single RF excitation, is the free induction decay (FID) introduced in @?fig-ch05-panel-fid.

title: 8  T2 Relaxation and Signal Contrast
section: 8.4 The two mechanisms of spin de-phasing
text:
8.4 The two mechanisms of spin de-phasing







Figure 8.3: Two sources of transverse magnetization decay: interactions between neighboring spins (top), and differences in the local magnetic field from one position to another (bottom).



Why do the spins lose their coherence? Glad you asked. There are two main reasons, and the distinction between them matters (Figure 8.3).

Spin-spin interactions (pure T2). Each proton is itself a tiny magnet, so every spin precesses in a field that is slightly perturbed by its neighbors. Because the molecules are tumbling, those perturbations fluctuate rapidly and randomly. Each spin’s precession rate wanders a little, the phase differences that accumulate are random, and coherence is lost for good. This contribution is irreversible: no later pulse can undo it.
Local field inhomogeneity (T2’). The static field is never perfectly uniform. Imperfections in the magnet, and — more important for the head — differences in magnetic susceptibility near the sinuses, the ear canals, and blood vessels, mean that spins at different positions sit in slightly different values of B0. They precess at slightly different but constant rates, and so they fan out steadily. This contribution is reversible, which is the trick behind the spin echo (?fig-ch09-pulse-sequences-spin-echo-hahn).
crumbs: 8  T2 Relaxation and Signal Contrast

title: 8  T2 Relaxation and Signal Contrast
text:
8.5 T2, T2’ and T2*

Combining the two decaysThe same relationship using rates








Figure 8.4: The relationship between the T2 decay time constants: the combined (T2*) rate is the sum of the spin-spin (T2) and inhomogeneity (T2’) rates.











Figure 8.5: The same relationship written with relaxation rates, \(R = 1/T\).






The two mechanisms act at the same time, and it is their rates that add, not their time constants. The combined effect is called T2*,
\[
\frac{1}{T_2^{*}} = \frac{1}{T_2} + \frac{1}{T_2'}
\]
Because rates add, T2* is always shorter than T2. The FID we actually measure therefore decays faster than the pure spin-spin relaxation would predict — which is why an FID by itself does not measure T2.
People don’t like all that one over stuff, so they use R1 to refer to 1 over T1, and R2 to refer to 1 over T2. In that notation the relationship is just \(R_2^{*} = R_2 + R_2'\). The equation looks simpler. It’s not.
crumbs: 8  T2 Relaxation and Signal Contrast

title: 8  T2 Relaxation and Signal Contrast
text:
8.6 Comparing T1 and T2 images
It is very unusual for investigators to acquire a pure T1 or a pure T2 image. Usually the image reflects relatively more of one than the other, and so we call it T1-weighted or T2-weighted. The timing of the pulse sequence is what sets the balance, and that is the subject of the next chapter.

8.6.1 T1-weighted images: gray is darker than white






Figure 8.6: T1-weighted images: gray is darker than white.



In a T1-weighted image, the signal is larger where T1 is shorter: tissue with a short T1 has recovered more of its longitudinal magnetization by the time we read the signal out. White matter has the shorter T1 (0.65 s, versus 0.88 s for gray matter at 1.5 T; Figure 7.11), so white matter is bright and gray matter is dark. CSF has the longest T1 of the three and is darkest of all — look at the ventricles in the coronal image. This is the contrast that makes T1-weighted volumes the standard anatomical image for separating gray from white matter.
The image in Figure 8.6 is from UCSD.



8.6.2 T2-weighted images: white is darker than gray






Figure 8.7: T2-weighted images: white is darker than gray.



T2-weighted images reverse this relationship. Now the signal is larger where T2 is longer, because tissue whose transverse magnetization decays slowly still has signal left when we measure it. At 3 T the average T2 is about 108 ms for gray matter and 78 ms for white matter, so gray matter is now the brighter of the two. CSF, with a T2 of roughly two seconds, is brighter still.
Figure 8.6 and Figure 8.7 are coronal images of the same subject, acquired in the same session. Comparing them is the quickest way to see the point of this chapter: the anatomy is the same and the contrast is inverted, because the two acquisitions are sensitive to different physical mechanisms.
Images from this UCSD site.

title: 8  T2 Relaxation and Signal Contrast
section: 8.8 T2-weighted images measure pathologies involving fluid filled regions
text:
8.8 T2-weighted images measure pathologies involving fluid filled regions






Figure 8.8: T2-weighted images measure pathologies involving fluid filled regions.



Free water has a much longer T2 than either gray or white matter (?fig-ch08-t2-time-course-and-t2-contrast). Many pathologies — edema, inflammation, cysts, tumors, vascular malformations — raise the local water content, so they stand out as conspicuously bright regions on a T2-weighted image. The arrow in the lower right panel marks an arteriovenous malformation (AVM).
Two cautions about the tissue values quoted here. First, the T2 of gray and white matter varies across the brain, so the averages are only a guide. Second, and more fundamental: a T2-weighted signal level is not itself a measurement of T2, because the signal also depends on proton density and on coil sensitivity. Turning the weighted image into a quantitative T2 map requires more than one measurement, which is the topic of the next chapter.
Reference values for normal tissue at 3 T are from Wansapura et al., NMR relaxation times in the human brain at 3.0 Tesla, J. Magn. Reson. Imaging 9:531-538 (1999), and from Konar et al., Quantitative relaxometry metrics for brain metastases compared to normal tissues, Cancers 14:5606 (2022), the source cited on the slide.

text:
8.9 Pulse sequence impact on tumor visibility






Figure 8.9: Pulse sequence impact on tumor visibility: (a) coronal image of the brain showing a tumor (arrow), bright against the darker grey of normal brain tissue; (b) the same slice with a different pulse sequence, showing the tumor darker than the surrounding brain (McRobbie et al., MRI: From Picture to Proton, 2e, Fig. 3.1).



The same tumor in the same slice can be brighter or darker than the surrounding brain, depending only on the pulse sequence used to acquire the image. Nothing about the tissue changed between the two panels; what changed is which relaxation mechanism the measurement was made sensitive to. Choosing that weighting deliberately, rather than accidentally, is what the next chapter is about.

title: 9  Spin Echo
text:
9.1 Pulse sequences: Spin echo (Hahn)
In our last two chapters, we explored T1 and T2 relaxation separately. But in real MR experiments, you’ll typically see both effects mixed together!
The magic happens in what we call the “pulse sequence” - the carefully timed dance of RF pulses and gradients that determines how these relaxation effects combine.
In this chapter, we’ll dive into one of MRI’s most important tricks: the spin echo. You’ll see how we use multiple RF pulses to isolate the T2 signal in a simple experiment that’s as elegant as the FID we started with.

title: 9  Spin Echo
section: 9.2 The RF pulse sequence up to now (FID)
text:
9.2 The RF pulse sequence up to now (FID)






Figure 9.1: The RF pulse sequence up to now (FID).



After the RF excitation pulse, we can measure a macroscopic signal (the FID). That’s a start. But notice that the signal starts very quickly and decayse very quickly. That makes it hard to instrument in real applications, particularly ones where we have to make a lot of measurements, say scanning a volume.

title: 9  Spin Echo
text:
9.3 Spin Echo (Hahn)






Figure 9.2: Spin Echo (Hahn).



The Hahn echo was not only a method to remove static dephasing; it introduced the idea that magnetic resonance signals could be engineered in time, allowing detection to be separated from excitation. This temporal separation was essential for overcoming hardware limitations and made practical NMR—and later MRI—possible.
For the original papers and biographical material, see the resource Erwin L. Hahn and the Spin Echo.

Figure 9.3: Demo by instructor and class spinning.
