title: 52  Arterial Spin Labeling and Quantitative Susceptibility Mapping
text:
52.2 Quantitative susceptibility mapping
Magnetic susceptibility (χ) measures how strongly a material becomes magnetized in an applied field, χ = M/H. It is helpful to picture the material as filled with tiny compass needles. Paramagnetic materials — deoxyhemoglobin, ferritin, some neurotransmitters — weakly align with the field (χ > 0). Diamagnetic materials — oxyhemoglobin, water, lipids, many proteins — weakly oppose it (χ < 0). Ferromagnetic materials such as iron align strongly and can stay aligned when the field is removed, but these are not found in the brain. Because myelin is diamagnetic and iron-bearing molecules are paramagnetic, a map of susceptibility carries information about both.
The complication is that susceptibility is not measured directly. What the scanner records is the phase of the signal, which reflects the local field perturbation produced by the susceptibility distribution — and that perturbation is spatially spread out, not localized to the source. Quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) begins by keeping the phase and amplitude from each receive coil and combining them as complex numbers, rather than forming the usual weighted sum of magnitudes (Figure 52.4). A naive complex sum without phase correction can cancel to zero where the coil phases disagree, so careful phase handling is central to the method.






Figure 52.4: QSM retains the phase and amplitude of each coil and combines them as a complex exponential. Without phase correction the complex sum can cancel to zero magnitude.



The heart of QSM is an inversion. The measured field perturbation is related to the underlying susceptibility distribution by a known physical forward model; QSM runs that model backward — a “field-to-source inversion” — to convert the spatial field measurement into a spatial estimate of susceptibility. For a single susceptibility source the field perturbation has the characteristic dipole pattern, and the inversion recovers a compact source (Figure 52.5). The same inversion applied voxel-by-voxel yields a whole-brain susceptibility map (Figure 52.6).






Figure 52.5: The core QSM calculation for a single source. The measured field perturbation (a dipole pattern) is inverted through the physical forward model to estimate the susceptibility.









Figure 52.6: Applying the field-to-source inversion across the whole brain produces a susceptibility map.



Clinically, QSM is attractive because susceptibility tracks iron deposition and myelin loss. In multiple sclerosis, for example, the susceptibility map delineates deep gray-matter structures and lesion cores more cleanly than the raw phase image, whose nonlocal contrast smears the lesion edge (Figure 52.7).






Figure 52.7: QSM in multiple sclerosis. Compared with the magnitude and phase images, the susceptibility map gives cleaner delineation of deep gray matter and a sharper lesion core.



A practical caution runs through the QSM literature: the inversion is ill-posed, and there are many algorithmic choices — regularization, background field removal, and so on — with active debate about which are correct. Community reconstruction challenges exist precisely to compare them. It is a good place to remember Box and Draper’s aphorism that all models are wrong, but some are useful (Figure 52.8).






Figure 52.8: There are many QSM reconstruction algorithms and ongoing debate about which is correct; community challenges compare them.
crumbs: 52  Arterial Spin Labeling and Quantitative Susceptibility Mapping

title: 53  VASO, Multi-echo, and MR Fingerprinting
text:
53.1 VASO
Vascular-space-occupancy (VASO) imaging, developed by van Zijl and colleagues, is a functional method aimed at improving the spatial specificity of fMRI (Figure 53.1). It exploits the fact that the T1 of blood differs from the T1 of brain parenchyma. By timing an inversion pulse to null the blood signal, VASO suppresses the contribution from within the vessels while sparing the tissue signal. Changes in the nulled signal then track changes in blood volume, a different physiological variable than the blood-oxygenation change that drives BOLD.
crumbs: 53  VASO, Multi-echo, and MR Fingerprinting

title: 53  VASO, Multi-echo, and MR Fingerprinting
text: Figure 53.1: VASO uses an inversion pulse timed to null the blood signal — possible because blood and parenchyma have different T1 — so that the measured change reflects blood volume.
crumbs: 53  VASO, Multi-echo, and MR Fingerprinting

title: 53  VASO, Multi-echo, and MR Fingerprinting
text:
53.2 Multi-echo imaging
An ordinary gradient-echo measures the signal at a single echo time, so the value it reports mixes two things: the starting magnetization S₀ (set by proton density and by transmit/receive coil sensitivity) and the T2* decay. That is why a plain T2*-weighted image is not quantitative — the absolute signal level at a given echo time differs from place to place even when the underlying decay constant is the same (Figure 53.2). What is comparable across locations is the time constant of the decay, not the signal level at one instant.






Figure 53.2: The measured signal at a fixed echo time depends on both S₀ and T2*. Because proton density and coil inhomogeneity make S₀ vary across the brain, the signal level is not comparable between locations; the T2* time constant is.



Multi-echo acquisition addresses this by reading out the same excitation at several echo times (Figure 53.3). Fitting the exponential decay across echoes separates the two quantities, producing an S₀ map and a T2* map (Figure 53.4). This separation is valuable for denoising functional data: BOLD is nominally a T2* change, but real signals also contain S₀ fluctuations that are artifactual, and having both maps lets one be removed to clean up the other.






Figure 53.3: The same slice acquired at increasing echo times (TE = 15, 31, 48 ms). The contrast changes systematically with echo time as the signal decays.









Figure 53.4: Fitting the decay across echoes yields separate S₀ and T2* maps from the same multi-echo data.
crumbs: 53  VASO, Multi-echo, and MR Fingerprinting

title: 53  VASO, Multi-echo, and MR Fingerprinting
text:
53.3 MR fingerprinting
MR fingerprinting (MRF), introduced by Ma and colleagues (Ma et al., 2013, Nature), inverts the usual logic of an MR experiment. Rather than tuning the sequence to produce one contrast, MRF drives the tissue with a deliberately varied, pseudo-random sequence so that each tissue type produces a distinctive signal “fingerprint” over time. Matching each measured fingerprint against a precomputed dictionary of simulated signals then yields several tissue parameters at once — T1, T2, and others — and, because the matching tolerates imperfections, it suppresses measurement error rather than propagating it (Figure 53.5).






Figure 53.5: The MR fingerprinting proposal: a single varied acquisition, matched against simulated signals, quantifies multiple tissue properties simultaneously.



In practice the acquisition is an ordinary pulse sequence — RF pulses, slice selection, and a readout — but with the flip angle and repetition time changed from one excitation to the next, and an efficient (often spiral) k-space trajectory (Figure 53.6). The key design choice is the schedule of flip angles and repetition times: a pseudo-random schedule (Figure 53.7) makes different tissues follow visibly different signal trajectories.






Figure 53.6: An MRF acquisition. The flip angle and repetition time vary across excitations, read out along a spiral k-space trajectory.









Figure 53.7: The flip-angle and repetition-time schedules are pseudo-random. Two example schedules are shown; the varied parameters are what give each tissue a distinctive signal.



The readout step is a simulation-and-match. The expected signal trajectory for each candidate substrate — white matter, gray matter, CSF, fat, off-resonance variants — is simulated in advance, and the measured signal is assigned to whichever simulated trajectory it matches best (Figure 53.8). The same simulation-based reconstruction idea has been used more narrowly to get fast, accurate quantitative T2 maps from multi-spin-echo data, correcting for the stimulated and indirect echoes that otherwise contaminate rapid protocols.






Figure 53.8: Different substrates produce distinct simulated signals (top); the measured signal is matched to the best-fitting simulated trajectory (bottom).
crumbs: 53  VASO, Multi-echo, and MR Fingerprinting

title: 54  High Field Imaging Challenges
text:
54.1 The resolution payoff
The clearest motivation for higher field is spatial detail. Comparing the same volunteer’s brain at 3 T and 9.4 T, the higher field resolves fine cortical and vascular structure that is blurred at the lower field (Figure 54.1). At 9.4 T, whole-brain gradient-echo images can reach in-plane resolutions of a few hundred micrometers (Figure 54.2), and susceptibility-weighted acquisitions resolve venous vasculature in exquisite detail (Figure 54.3).

title: 54  High Field Imaging Challenges
text:
Figure 54.1: The brain of one volunteer imaged at 3 T (left) and 9.4 T (right). The higher field supports substantially finer spatial resolution.









Figure 54.2: A sagittal gradient-echo image at 9.4 T with whole-brain coverage, roughly 280 µm in-plane and 1 mm thick, acquired in about five and a half minutes. The transmit phases of the 16 elements were optimized for this slice.









Figure 54.3: Susceptibility-weighted imaging at 9.4 T, here about 0.175 mm in-plane, resolves fine venous structure.

title: 54  High Field Imaging Challenges
text:
54.2 The instrumentation challenge
The reason ultra-high-field imaging is hard is that the RF wavelength shrinks as field strength rises. At 9.4 T the wavelength in tissue is comparable to the size of the head, so a single transmit coil can no longer produce a uniform excitation — the transmit field (\(B_1^+\)) becomes patchy, brightening and darkening across the brain. The response is parallel transmission: an array of independently driven transmit elements whose phases (and amplitudes) are adjusted to shape the excitation, as in the 16-element system used for the images above. The caption’s remark that the transmit phases “were optimized for this slice” reflects exactly this — the excitation has to be tuned, sometimes per slice, to achieve uniformity.
Building such arrays is a hardware problem in its own right. Each element needs integrated transmit/receive switches and preamplifiers so the same coil can both transmit and receive (Figure 54.4). Even with all of this, the images typically require intensity correction after the fact to compensate for the residual non-uniform sensitivity — the 9.4 T images above are explicitly noted as non-intensity-corrected, which is why their brightness varies across the field of view. High field buys resolution, but only after the transmit-uniformity and coil-engineering problems are solved.






Figure 54.4: Transmit-array hardware for high-field imaging. Integrated transmit/receive switches with preamplifiers let the array operate in transceive mode.

title: 55  Macromolecular Tissue Volume and the g-ratio
text:
55.1 Macromolecular tissue volume
The motivation for MTV is microstructural. A very small part of a white-matter voxel contains axons wrapped in many layers of myelin, and each myelin membrane is a lipid bilayer surrounded by water (Figure 55.1). The more myelin and other macromolecular material a voxel contains, the less room is left for water. If we can measure the water fraction accurately, then one minus that fraction — the macromolecular tissue volume — is a measure of tissue content.
The water fraction is estimated from proton density (PD), and here the practical difficulty appears. Raw scanner images are not quantitative: their brightness falls off systematically from the center to the edge because of the receive coil’s spatially varying sensitivity (Figure 55.2). Recovering a true PD map means separating this coil gain from the tissue signal, not merely cosmetically flattening the image.
The starting point is quantitative T1 mapping. A single T1-weighted image confounds the tissue’s T1 with the scan parameters and coil gain; acquiring several images at different flip angles and fitting the spoiled gradient-echo signal equation separates these factors, yielding clean T1 and PD (M0) maps (Figure 55.3). The image intensity can be written schematically as a function of coil gain, scan parameters, and tissue properties, and the fit disentangles them.
Estimating PD from the data is an ill-posed problem, and it is instructive to see why. In simulation without noise the coil sensitivity and PD can be recovered perfectly; add realistic noise and the estimates degrade badly, because a flexible model fits the noise rather than the signal, and the cross-validation accuracy collapses (Figure 55.4). The remedy is regularization: adding a constraint from something else we know to be true. Here the useful prior is the physical relationship between T1 and PD, which lets a biophysically regularized fit recover accurate PD maps.
Is the resulting MTV a genuine measure of tissue volume, independent of the particular chemistry? A calibration experiment says largely yes. Working with the chemistry department to build lipid phantoms — with and without inserted cholesterol — the measured lipid volume tracks the calculated lipid volume along the line of identity regardless of whether cholesterol is present (Figure 55.5). MTV measures how much space the macromolecules occupy, not what they are made of.
Chemistry does leave a separate signature, however, in how strongly the water interacts with the macromolecular surfaces. The same tissue volume can produce a different surface-interaction rate. Defining the volume of interacting protons as \(VIP = (T1_m - T1_f)/(T1_c - T1_f)\) — where \(T1_m\) is the measured T1, \(T1_f\) the T1 of free water, and \(T1_c\) a calibration value — and the surface interaction rate as \(SIR = VIP/MTV\), cholesterol-containing samples show a higher interaction rate at the same lipid volume (Figure 55.6). MTV and SIR are complementary: one reports how much material is present, the other reports something about its surface chemistry.
crumbs: 55  Macromolecular Tissue Volume and the g-ratio

title: 55  Macromolecular Tissue Volume and the g-ratio
text:
Figure 55.1: A white-matter voxel is dominated by myelinated axons. Each myelin membrane is a lipid bilayer (~5 nm) surrounded by water (~1 nm layers); more myelin means less space for water.










Figure 55.2: A raw T1-weighted image. Brightness varies from edge to center because of the receive coil’s spatially varying sensitivity — an artifact that must be removed quantitatively to estimate proton density.










Figure 55.3: Quantitative T1. The same brain at several flip angles shows that intensity depends on scan parameters as well as tissue T1. Fitting the signal equation across flip angles separates coil gain, T1, and proton density.










Figure 55.4: Overfitting in PD estimation. Without noise the fit is perfect (top); with noise, an unconstrained fit tracks the noise and fails (bottom). A regularization constraint is needed.










Figure 55.5: Lipid-phantom calibration. Measured lipid volume matches calculated lipid volume along the identity line whether or not cholesterol is added, showing that MTV is largely insensitive to lipid chemistry.










Figure 55.6: Same volume, different signature. VIP/SIR increases with cholesterol at matched lipid volume, so the surface-interaction rate carries chemical information beyond the volume itself.




55.1.1 Why not just use diffusion?
The usual way to characterize white matter is diffusion imaging, but FA is not a clean measure of tissue content. FA varies enormously along a single tract, and the largest swings come from geometry — crossing fibers — rather than from myelin. Where callosal fibers cross the corticospinal tract, FA drops sharply, and the rank ordering of subjects changes from place to place along the tract (Figure 55.7). MTV is attractive precisely because it responds to tissue content more directly than FA does.






Figure 55.7: FA varies strongly along the corticospinal tract, dropping where callosal fibers cross it. The largest FA changes reflect fiber geometry, not tissue content.



Combining a tract model with quantitative maps gives tract profiles that can be compared against a normative range. In multiple sclerosis patients, the macromolecular tissue volume fraction (MTVF) along the corticospinal tract falls below the control distribution at specific locations, and the diffusion and FA profiles add complementary information about disease stage (Figure 55.8).






Figure 55.8: Tract profiles in two MS patients (red) against the control distribution (gray). MTVF, a diffusion index, and FA each drop below the normal range at particular tract locations.
crumbs: 55  Macromolecular Tissue Volume and the g-ratio

title: 55  Macromolecular Tissue Volume and the g-ratio
text:
55.2 The g-ratio
Myelin does two things for an axon: it speeds conduction and it lowers the energy cost of signaling. Conduction velocity rises with fiber caliber, but only for myelinated axons — the unmyelinated curve stays low across the whole range of diameters (Figure 55.9). The precise speed depends on how much myelin wraps a given axon.






Figure 55.9: Conduction speed versus fiber caliber. Myelinated fibers (upper curve) conduct far faster than unmyelinated fibers (lower curve), and the relationship depends on myelin amount.



The amount of myelin is not arbitrary: across axons there is a consistent relationship between myelin thickness and axon perimeter, so larger axons carry proportionally thicker sheaths (Figure 55.10). This regularity is captured by a single number, the g-ratio.






Figure 55.10: Myelin thickness scales with axon perimeter across a population of fibers (Fraher, 1972), motivating a single geometric summary — the g-ratio.



The g-ratio is the ratio of the inner (axon) to the outer (axon + myelin) diameter of a myelinated fiber (Figure 55.11). It matters because it sets the balance between conduction speed and the metabolic and spatial cost of myelin. It can be estimated from MRI by combining a myelin volume fraction (MVF) and an axon volume fraction (AVF): \(g = \sqrt{1/(1 + MVF/AVF)}\). In practice MVF comes from a myelin-sensitive measurement such as MTV or magnetization transfer, and AVF comes from a diffusion model that estimates the intra-axonal water fraction.






Figure 55.11: Geometry of the g-ratio, \(g = r/R = \sqrt{1/(1 + MVF/AVF)}\), with the tissue water compartments and their relaxation times. MVF is the myelin volume fraction; AVF is the axon volume fraction.



Putting these ingredients together yields whole-brain g-ratio maps from multi-shell diffusion plus a myelin measurement: separate MVF and AVF maps combine into a g-ratio map that is relatively uniform across healthy white matter (Figure 55.12). The clinical interest is that the g-ratio can distinguish kinds of tissue damage. In multiple sclerosis, lesions are hyperintense on FLAIR and reduced on both the MVF and AVF maps, but the g-ratio map — being a ratio — separates lesions in which myelin and axons are lost proportionally (g-ratio near normal) from the occasional lesion with disproportionate myelin loss (elevated g-ratio) (Figure 55.13).






Figure 55.12: Whole-brain g-ratio from multi-shell DWI. MVF and AVF maps combine into a g-ratio map that is fairly uniform across healthy white matter.









Figure 55.13: g-ratio in multiple sclerosis (Stikov et al., 2015). Lesions reduce MVF and AVF, but most retain a near-normal g-ratio; only one lesion here has a g-ratio above 0.8, indicating disproportionate myelin loss.
crumbs: 55  Macromolecular Tissue Volume and the g-ratio

title: 56  Topology, Statistical Parameter Mapping, and Surface Visualization
text:
56.1 Why visualization matters
Anscombe’s quartet is a classic illustration of a general danger: four data sets with identical summary statistics (mean, variance, correlation) can look completely different once plotted (Figure 56.1). The same danger applies to brain data — two very different patterns of activity or tissue structure can share the same summary numbers, so visualizing the data directly, not just its statistics, is an essential check.
Spatial resolution compounds this problem in the brain because of cortical folding. Two points that are close together in physical (Euclidean) space can be far apart along the folded cortical sheet, on opposite banks of a sulcus (Figure 56.2). Any analysis that treats nearby voxels as necessarily related is implicitly assuming a spatial smoothness that the folded anatomy does not actually have.
crumbs: 56  Topology, Statistical Parameter Mapping, and Surface Visualization

title: 56  Topology, Statistical Parameter Mapping, and Surface Visualization
text:
Figure 56.1: Anscombe’s quartet: four data sets with the same summary statistics but very different shapes when plotted.










Figure 56.2: Spatial proximity in a volume does not imply proximity along the cortical surface — brain folding brings distant regions of cortex physically close together.
crumbs: 56  Topology, Statistical Parameter Mapping, and Surface Visualization

title: 56  Topology, Statistical Parameter Mapping, and Surface Visualization
text:
56.2 Topology and visualization
A single MR slice can cut across a sulcus twice, sampling both banks in the same plane even though they are far apart along the cortical sheet — for example, a coronal slice through the calcarine sulcus includes tissue from both banks of the fold (Figure 56.3). This is the concrete anatomical reason topology matters: the natural neighborhood structure of the data is defined by the cortical surface, not by the Euclidean geometry of the acquired volume.






Figure 56.3: A coronal MR slice through the calcarine sulcus. The dotted line marks the slice plane; an MR slice through the blue line would include parts of opposite banks of the sulcus.
crumbs: 56  Topology, Statistical Parameter Mapping, and Surface Visualization

title: 56  Topology, Statistical Parameter Mapping, and Surface Visualization
section: 56.3 Matching data methods to what you are studying
text:
56.3 Matching data methods to what you are studying
Thinking about the natural shape and organization of the problem you are studying is important. Mathematical theorems about smoothing and averaging are very useful, but every problem has its own special features, and being sensitive to them is essential — spatial averaging in the brain is a good example. A smoothing kernel applied in volume space averages together whatever voxels fall within its radius, regardless of whether those voxels belong to the same fold of cortex.

Grid of samplesSelecting a pair of nodesThe averaging kernel








Figure 56.4: A regular grid of sample locations overlaid on an axial slice.











Figure 56.5: Two neighboring grid nodes are selected.











Figure 56.6: A circular averaging kernel is centered on the selected nodes.






The trouble is visible as soon as the kernel straddles a sulcus. Opposite banks of a sulcus can be very close together in volume space yet functionally distinct — one bank gray matter, the other white matter, or two banks belonging to different functional maps — so opposite sides of sulci can’t be distinguished by a purely volumetric criterion (Figure 56.7). The figure shown in-plane is only a 2D cross-section; the averaging itself happens in the full 3D volume, which makes the problem worse, not better.






Figure 56.7: Opposite banks of a sulcus can be indistinguishable in volume space: white matter and gray matter from both banks can fall within the same local neighborhood. The averaging kernel operates in the volume even though only an in-plane slice is shown.



Smoothing therefore averages together signal from tissue that may not belong together at all (Figure 56.8) — the same sulcus-crossing problem, now shown as it would appear after a smoothing kernel has been applied at several locations along a fold.






Figure 56.8: What is actually averaged by smoothing: circles mark local regions where the kernel mixes signal across opposite banks of a sulcus.
crumbs: 56  Topology, Statistical Parameter Mapping, and Surface Visualization

title: 56  Topology, Statistical Parameter Mapping, and Surface Visualization
text:
56.4 Statistical parameter mapping
Statistical parameter maps (SPMs) render a statistical test (for example, a t- or F-statistic computed at every voxel) as a color overlay on an anatomical image. An older convention in the literature — one that can still be found in some papers — displayed these overlays on a small number of 2D slices, which is a visualization choice worth being alert to when reading older figures, since it can make results look more (or less) spatially extensive than they are.
Spatial smoothing is applied before statistical testing for several distinct reasons, and it is worth separating them out:

(i) Matched filter theorem(ii) Central limit theorem(iii) Gaussian random field theory(iv) Inter-subject averaging


By the matched filter theorem, the optimal smoothing kernel size matches the expected spatial size of the effect being tested — smoothing at the wrong scale reduces sensitivity.






Figure 56.9: Motivation (i): the matched filter theorem sets the optimal smoothing kernel size.





By the central limit theorem, smoothing renders the noise distribution more Gaussian, which helps satisfy the assumptions behind parametric statistical tests.






Figure 56.10: Motivation (ii): smoothing makes the error distribution more normal.





Inferences about regional effects that rely on Gaussian random field theory assume the underlying statistical field is smooth; explicit smoothing helps satisfy that assumption.






Figure 56.11: Motivation (iii): Gaussian random field theory assumes a smooth statistical field.





When averaging across subjects — whose anatomy never aligns perfectly — more aggressive smoothing (e.g., 8 mm in fMRI, 16 mm in PET) is often needed to project individual results onto a common space.






Figure 56.12: Motivation (iv): heavier smoothing compensates for imperfect inter-subject alignment.






Each of these is a legitimate reason to smooth, but each also trades away some spatial specificity — precisely the specificity that the sulcus-crossing problem above shows can matter a great deal in folded cortex.
crumbs: 56  Topology, Statistical Parameter Mapping, and Surface Visualization

title: 56  Topology, Statistical Parameter Mapping, and Surface Visualization
text:
56.5 Surface-based visualization
Visualization exists to communicate results clearly, and the choice of surface matters as much as the statistics. The same activation can look very different rendered on a small number of thick axial slices versus rendered on a 3D cortical surface reconstruction (Figure 56.13).






Figure 56.13: The same statistical result shown (a) on thick axial slices and (b) rendered on a 3D cortical surface — the surface rendering communicates the spatial extent of the activation far more clearly.



Cortical surface projections are commonly shown from standard viewpoints, such as the lateral surface and the ventral occipital surface, so that results from different studies and subjects can be compared directly (Figure 56.14, Figure 56.15).






Figure 56.14: A lateral surface projection of the cortex (data from Brunswick and Paulesu).









Figure 56.15: A ventral occipital view of the cortical surface.



A concrete example of why this matters: interpreting results shown in a conventional multi-slice format is hard, even for an experienced reader (Figure 56.16). The same visual word form area data, replotted on a 3D cortical surface reconstruction, is much easier to interpret — the contrast showing an increasing response as a word form becomes more visible is immediately legible as a single, spatially coherent region rather than scattered patches across several slices (Figure 56.17).






Figure 56.16: Multi-slice format visualization is a challenge to understand: color indicates stimulus eccentricity, but the spatial pattern is hard to read across slices.









Figure 56.17: The same data shown on a 3D surface reconstruction: the visual word form area is much easier to see than in the multi-slice view.
crumbs: 56  Topology, Statistical Parameter Mapping, and Surface Visualization

title: 56  Topology, Statistical Parameter Mapping, and Surface Visualization
text:
56.6 Building the cortical surface
To build a representation of the cortical surface, the anatomical MRI volume is segmented into gray and white matter, and the boundary between them is identified. A variety of software tools do this segmentation; here the boundary is shown as identified by itkGray, one of several available pipelines (others include FreeSurfer) (Figure 56.18; Carman et al. (1995); Dale et al. (1999); Fischl et al. (1999); Wandell et al. (2000)).






Figure 56.18: Identifying the gray-white boundary in cortex using itkGray.



Automatic segmentation is an excellent first approximation and very useful in practice (Figure 56.19), but there are always imperfections that need to be checked and, often, hand-corrected (Figure 56.20).






Figure 56.19: Automatic gray/white segmentation: an excellent first approximation and very useful on its own.









Figure 56.20: But there are always imperfections that need checking.



Once the voxels are classified as gray or white matter, they must be connected into a well-formed graph before a surface mesh can be built. Gray matter nodes are considered connected if they share a common parent voxel or if their parents are connected, and the classification, connectivity, and resulting cortical graph are all closely linked (Figure 56.21).






Figure 56.21: Classification, connectivity, and the resulting graph of gray-matter nodes.



A well-formed white-matter classification must also avoid topological defects — cavities (holes enclosed by white matter) and handles (spurious connections that create a loop where none should exist). The Euler number is a standard way of detecting the presence of such defects (Figure 56.22; Toriwaki & Yonekura (2002)).






Figure 56.22: White matter topology: avoiding cavities and handles. The Euler number detects topological defects in the classified volume.
crumbs: 56  Topology, Statistical Parameter Mapping, and Surface Visualization

title: 56  Topology, Statistical Parameter Mapping, and Surface Visualization
section: 56.7 From classified voxels to a mesh
text:
56.7 From classified voxels to a mesh
Graphics programs represent surfaces as meshes: a set of vertices (points) and edges (connections between them). A mesh can be built directly from the boundary of the classified white-matter voxels (Figure 56.23).






Figure 56.23: Creating the surface mesh from classified voxels.



Representing the cortex as a mesh matters for more than visualization: the same mesh that renders the surface for viewing (in tools such as MeshLab) also encodes the gray-matter connectivity graph used for measurement, so a properly connected mesh is required both for pictures that look right and for distances and areas that are computed correctly (Figure 56.24).






Figure 56.24: The importance of being a mesh: a single mesh structure supports both visualization and correct gray-node connectivity.



A raw mesh built directly from voxel boundaries is jagged; 3D graphical tools (such as VTK, the Visualization Toolkit) can smooth the mesh without destroying the topological neighborhood relations of the surface (Figure 56.25). Modern segmentation and meshing tools such as itkGray increasingly build in this kind of anatomical and topological knowledge automatically, though getting good results still requires practice (Figure 56.26).






Figure 56.25: Smoothing the 3D mesh with tools such as VTK, preserving the surface’s topological properties.









Figure 56.26: Tissue classification tools such as itkGray incorporate increasingly sophisticated anatomical knowledge.
crumbs: 56  Topology, Statistical Parameter Mapping, and Surface Visualization

title: 56  Topology, Statistical Parameter Mapping, and Surface Visualization
text:
56.8 Curvature and extreme smoothing
Shading a rendered surface by local curvature makes the gyri and sulci easy to read at a glance: curvature is inversely related to the radius of the circle that best fits the local surface (Figure 56.27). Even after very heavy smoothing, the mesh’s topology — its neighborhood connectivity — remains unchanged; only the geometry (the shape) is altered, not the underlying graph structure (Figure 56.28).






Figure 56.27: Shading the surface by curvature: high curvature marks tightly folded gyri and sulci, low curvature marks flatter regions.









Figure 56.28: Extreme smoothing changes the surface’s shape but leaves its topology unchanged.
crumbs: 56  Topology, Statistical Parameter Mapping, and Surface Visualization

title: 56  Topology, Statistical Parameter Mapping, and Surface Visualization
text:
56.9 Flat maps
Because the cortical sheet is topologically close to a 2D surface, it can be cut and unfolded into a flat map — a representation that preserves neighborhood relations along the cortical surface far better than any single volumetric slice can. Flattened representations are especially useful for displaying data that vary smoothly across the surface, such as eccentricity maps from retinotopic mapping experiments (Figure 56.29, Figure 56.30, Figure 56.31).






Figure 56.29: An eccentricity map shown on the folded cortical surface.









Figure 56.30: A flat-map view of the brain surface.









Figure 56.31: The same eccentricity map shown on the flattened representation.



No flattening is perfect, however. The cortical surface has intrinsic curvature, which limits how well distances measured on the flattened image can match true distances on the folded surface — even a surface that is basically flat, and not strongly curved like a sphere, will not be perfectly representable on a plane without some distortion (Figure 56.32). The next chapter takes up the flattening procedure itself in detail.






Figure 56.32: Intrinsic curvature limits how well distances on a flattened image can match true distances on the cortical surface.








Carman, G. J., Drury, H. A., & Van Essen, D. C. (1995). Computational methods for reconstructing and unfolding the cerebral cortex. Cerebral Cortex, 5(6), 506–517. https://doi.org/10.1093/cercor/5.6.506


Dale, A. M., Fischl, B., & Sereno, M. I. (1999). Cortical surface-based analysis i: Segmentation and surface reconstruction. NeuroImage, 9(2), 179–194. https://doi.org/10.1006/nimg.1998.0395


Fischl, B., Sereno, M. I., & Dale, A. M. (1999). Cortical surface-based analysis II: Inflation, flattening, and a surface-based coordinate system. NeuroImage, 9(2), 195–207. https://doi.org/10.1006/nimg.1998.0396


Toriwaki, J., & Yonekura, T. (2002). Euler number and connectivity indexes of a three dimensional digital picture. Forma, 17(3), 183–209.


Wandell, B. A., Chial, S., & Backus, B. T. (2000). Visualization and measurement of the cortical surface. Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience, 12(5), 739–752. https://doi.org/10.1162/089892900562561
crumbs: 56  Topology, Statistical Parameter Mapping, and Surface Visualization

title: 57  Cortical Flattening and the Marching Cubes Algorithm
text:
57.1 Flattening the cortical surface
Gray-matter nodes on the cortical mesh have 3D positions \((x, y, z)\); the goal of flattening is to assign each node a 2D position \((u, v)\) in an image plane while preserving, as much as possible, the neighborhood relations of the original mesh. The method used here follows a principle developed by W.T. Tutte (1960): place each node at the average position of its connected neighbors, and no folds are introduced into the surface this way (Figure 57.1; Tutte (1963)).
The important practical point is that this averaging condition is a linear system. If \(\mathbf{X}\) holds the 2D positions of the interior nodes and \(\mathbf{X}_0\) the fixed positions of the perimeter nodes, the condition that each interior node sits at the average of its neighbors is written \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{N}\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{P}\mathbf{X}_0\), where \(\mathbf{N}\) is a node-connection matrix (normalized by each node’s number of connections) and \(\mathbf{P}\) plays the same role for perimeter connections. Solving for \(\mathbf{X}\) gives \(\mathbf{X} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{N})^{-1}
\mathbf{P}\mathbf{X}_0\) — a single linear solve places every interior node at once, in a way that preserves the mesh’s topology (Figure 57.2).
In practice, once a segmentation exists, flattening a patch of cortex is straightforward: select a start point on the mesh, select a distance (radius) defining how much of the mesh to unfold, and run the algorithm (Figure 57.3). Tools such as mrFlatMesh implement this directly: they read in the gray-matter mesh, take a start point and a radius, and solve the flattening equations (Figure 57.4).
The result can be inspected directly: the mesh triangles end up on the plane without any edge crossings, confirming the flattening is valid, though the triangles are not uniformly positioned across the flattened patch (Figure 57.5). Two further quantities are typically computed and displayed alongside the flattened mesh: a manifold distance map (geodesic distance from the starting point, measured along the original surface) and a curvature map, which together let a viewer judge how much the flattening has distorted the true surface (Figure 57.6).

text:
Figure 57.1: Flattening a cortical mesh follows Tutte’s principle: place each node at the average position of its connected neighbors.










Figure 57.2: The matrix form of the flattening equation: node positions are found by solving one linear system.










Figure 57.3: Flattening tools: given a segmentation, select a start point and a radius, then run the algorithm.









Figure 57.4: mrFlatMesh: a graphical tool for flattening a patch of the gray-matter mesh.

title: 57  Cortical Flattening and the Marching Cubes Algorithm
section: 57.2 Marching squares: finding a boundary curve
text:
57.2 Marching squares: finding a boundary curve
Both flattening and mesh construction depend on a more basic operation: extracting a boundary (in 2D) or a surface (in 3D) from a classified grid of samples. In two dimensions this is the marching squares algorithm. Each grid node is classified as inside or outside the shape (green vertices inside, in this illustration); new vertices are placed at the midpoint of each in/out pair of neighboring grid nodes (red), and the boundary is drawn through those new vertices.

Classified gridDrawing the boundaryLocal configurations








Figure 57.7: A regular grid of sample points classified as inside (green) or outside a shape.











Figure 57.8: New vertices (red) are placed at the midpoint of each in/out pair, and the boundary is drawn through them.











Figure 57.9: Only a small number of distinct local line configurations are possible, each a rotation of one of four basic cases.






The result is an “OK” but visibly jagged representation of the true boundary — the polygon approximation is more angular than the underlying shape, so some form of boundary smoothing is required. One simple approach: find the curve normals at each vertex, smooth the way their orientation changes along the curve, and reconstruct the curve from the smoothed normals (Figure 57.10).






Figure 57.10: Boundary smoothing: find the curve normals, smooth their orientation change, and reconstruct the curve from the smoothed normals.
crumbs: 57  Cortical Flattening and the Marching Cubes Algorithm

title: 57  Cortical Flattening and the Marching Cubes Algorithm
section: 57.3 Marching cubes: finding a surface in 3D
text:
57.3 Marching cubes: finding a surface in 3D
Marching cubes is the natural three-dimensional generalization of marching squares, and it is the standard algorithm for extracting a surface mesh from a classified 3D volume such as a segmented gray/white matter volume (Lorensen & Cline (1987)). Each cube (formed by eight neighboring voxel corners) has its corners classified as above or below an isovalue; since there are 8 corners, there are \(2^8 = 256\) possible corner classifications, and the algorithm must determine which section (or sections) of surface divides each cube accordingly.

Classifying cube cornersThe 15 distinct cube combinationsSymmetry reduces the cases further








Figure 57.11: Each of a cube’s 8 corners is classified as inside or outside the isosurface, giving 256 possible configurations.











Figure 57.12: After removing trivial (all-in or all-out) cases, 15 distinct surface configurations remain; edge-intersection points determine how the surface cuts through each cube.











Figure 57.13: Rotation about any of the 3 primary axes, mirroring, and corner-state inversion relate many of the 15 combinations to each other, so only a handful of truly distinct cases must be handled explicitly.






Increasing the point-sampling density improves the smoothness of the resulting mesh but does not, by itself, solve the fundamental jaggedness problem — the surface is still built from flat triangular facets, just more of them (Figure 57.14).






Figure 57.14: Increasing point-sampling density improves resolution but does not solve the fundamental faceting problem.
crumbs: 57  Cortical Flattening and the Marching Cubes Algorithm

title: 57  Cortical Flattening and the Marching Cubes Algorithm
text:
57.4 Connectivity, revisited
Both marching squares and marching cubes depend on a definition of neighborhood connectivity among voxels, the same issue raised in the previous chapter’s discussion of white-matter topology. In 3D, the two common conventions are 6-connectivity (only face-adjacent neighbors) and 26-connectivity (all face-, edge-, and corner-adjacent neighbors) (Figure 57.15). The choice of connectivity convention affects which configurations are treated as topologically valid and is part of why the Euler-number bookkeeping introduced earlier matters in practice, not just in principle.






Figure 57.15: Common types of voxel connectivity: 6-neighborhood (face-adjacent only) versus 26-neighborhood (face, edge, and corner adjacent).








Lorensen, W. E., & Cline, H. E. (1987). Marching cubes: A high resolution 3D surface construction algorithm. Proceedings of the 14th Annual Conference on Computer Graphics and Interactive Techniques (SIGGRAPH ’87), 163–169. https://doi.org/10.1145/37401.37422


Tutte, W. T. (1963). How to draw a graph. Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society, s3-13(1), 743–767. https://doi.org/10.1112/plms/s3-13.1.743

title: 58  Segmentation and Visualization: Additional Examples
text:
58.1 Gray-white segmentation is essential
Every step in the surface-construction pipeline — meshing, smoothing, flattening — depends on an accurate gray/white matter segmentation as its starting point. Overlaying a sampling grid on an unsegmented axial slice (a) versus the same slice with the gray/white boundary traced (b) makes clear how much structure the segmentation step adds before any surface computation can begin (Figure 58.1).
Segmentation is typically done with dedicated tools such as itkGray (built on ITK-SNAP), which let a user inspect a volume in multiple planes simultaneously, draw and edit labels, and preview the resulting 3D region (Figure 58.2).

title: 58  Segmentation and Visualization: Additional Examples
text:
Figure 58.1: (a) An axial slice with a sampling grid overlaid, before segmentation. (b) The same slice with the gray/white matter boundary traced.










Figure 58.2: itkGray (built on ITK-SNAP), a segmentation tool showing axial, sagittal, and coronal views alongside a 3D preview.

title: 58  Segmentation and Visualization: Additional Examples
text:
58.2 Voxel size and resampling
Scanner voxels are frequently anisotropic — for example, \(0.9375 \times
0.9375 \times 1.2\) mm — and if the image is displayed without accounting for this, each measurement sample simply becomes one image pixel and the brain appears artificially “thin” (Figure 58.3).






Figure 58.3: The original scan represented as voxels with no scaling applied: each sample is one pixel, so the anisotropic \(0.9375 \times 0.9375 \times 1.2\)~mm voxels make the brain look thin.



Resampling to an isotropic (iso-)voxel size — for example, \(0.9 \times 0.9
\times 0.9\) mm — corrects this distortion, at the cost of introducing interpolation noise (Figure 58.4). Standard scattered-data and grid interpolation routines (such as MATLAB’s interp2 for 2D reslicing and TriScatteredInterp for scattered 3D data) are the practical tools used to perform this resampling.






Figure 58.4: Resampled to an isotropic \(0.9 \times 0.9 \times 0.9\)~mm voxel grid — note the interpolation noise introduced in the process.
crumbs: 58  Segmentation and Visualization: Additional Examples

title: 58  Segmentation and Visualization: Additional Examples
text:
58.3 Averaging multiple scans improves segmentation
Co-registering and averaging several repeated scans of the same subject reduces noise substantially before any segmentation is attempted (Figure 58.5).






Figure 58.5: Multiple scans of the same subject, co-registered and averaged.



The benefit shows up directly in the intensity histogram used to separate gray and white matter: averaging sharpens the separation between the gray and white matter intensity peaks, making automatic segmentation more reliable (Figure 58.6).






Figure 58.6: Averaging multiple scans sharpens the separation between gray- and white-matter intensity peaks, making segmentation easier.

title: Joseph Larmor and his frequency
text:
Work in Progress



Suggestions of all kinds for these lecture notes are welcome — whether it’s fixing small errors, raising bigger questions, or offering new perspectives. Please share comments through GitHub Issues. To make feedback easier to address, please point to the section you have in mind — by section number or a short snippet of text.








Figure 1: Joseph Larmor



Sir Joseph Larmor (11 July 1857–19 May 1942) was an Irish physicist and mathematician. His work ranged across electricity, dynamics, thermodynamics, and the electron theory of matter. Most important for MRI, he described the precession of a magnetic moment in an applied magnetic field: the relationship now known as the Larmor frequency. It is this relationship that determines the RF frequency required to excite hydrogen nuclei at a given \(B_0\) field strength.
Larmor’s most influential book, Aether and Matter (1900), set out his theoretical account of electricity and matter. It appeared five years before Einstein’s 1905 annus mirabilis papers, at a time when physicists were reconsidering the nature of space, time, and electromagnetic phenomena.
Larmor remained attached to the older aether-based picture of physics and was cautious about later developments, especially quantum theory and relativity. His response to Einstein’s theory of gravitation changed over time: he briefly accepted it, but later returned to a critical position. This historical context does not diminish the lasting importance of Larmor precession, which remains central to magnetic resonance.

title: Drawing Single NMR Spins
text:
Three useful representations
The alignment model emphasizes that a measurement of the spin component along the main field, \(B_0\), has two possible outcomes. At thermal equilibrium, a small population excess in the lower-energy state accounts for the nonzero longitudinal magnetization, \(M_0\).
The two-cone model represents a magnetic moment as precessing about \(B_0\). It provides useful geometric intuition for precession, but it is not a literal trajectory of an individual quantum spin.
The uniform model represents an ensemble with moments distributed over directions. It can be especially useful for visualizing phase coherence after excitation and the subsequent loss of coherence. As with the other models, its value is pedagogical: the quantum state, rather than a classical vector, is the underlying description of one proton.

title: Drawing Single NMR Spins
text:
Connection to the macroscopic model
MRI receiver coils do not observe individual spins. They record a voltage induced by the time-varying net transverse magnetization, \(M_{xy}\). The macroscopic model therefore focuses on the properties that determine that voltage: equilibrium magnetization, RF excitation, phase coherence, precession, and relaxation.
Williamson compares these representations in detail and argues for their complementary teaching roles (Williamson, 2019).





Williamson, M. P. (2019). Drawing single NMR spins and understanding relaxation. Natural Product Communications.

title: Why Spins Relax
text:
The question underneath this whole topic
Two papers on how to teach and think about NMR — Williamson (2019, “Drawing Single NMR Spins and Understanding Relaxation”) and Hanson (2008, “Is Quantum Mechanics Necessary for Understanding Magnetic Resonance?”) — both make a similar, somewhat provocative claim: most of what you need to understand about how nuclear spins behave in a magnetic field does not require quantum mechanics. Precession, resonance, the effect of RF pulses, even the shape of the equilibrium magnetization — all of this can be pictured with an ordinary classical vector, like a tiny bar magnet or a spinning top, and the classical picture is not just a simplification, it’s accurate.
But there’s one place both papers stop and say: here, you actually need quantum mechanics, and no classical picture gets it right. That place is relaxation — specifically the process called T1 relaxation, where a population of spins that starts out disturbed from equilibrium gradually settles back into a small net alignment with the magnetic field.
This summary walks through why the classical picture works as well as it does, and then pins down exactly where and why it breaks — because the “why” turns out to be genuinely interesting, and it’s not the reason people usually assume.

title: Why Spins Relax
section: Three ways to draw a spin (Williamson)
text:
Three ways to draw a spin (Williamson)
Williamson’s paper is about how NMR textbooks typically draw a single nuclear spin, and why two of the three standard pictures are actively misleading.
The alignment model. Spins point either straight along the field (+z) or straight against it (−z), like a two-state switch, with a slight statistical excess in the “with the field” state. This is the picture most people first learn, and it’s wrong in an important way: it implies each spin sits permanently in one of exactly two orientations, full stop.
The 2-cone model. Spins point somewhere on the surface of one of two cones tilted at the “magic angle” (about 54°) from the field, precessing around it. This one is popular in advanced texts and explains precession and phase, but it has the same underlying flaw as the alignment model — it still assumes every spin sits in one of exactly two possible orbits — and it leads to real contradictions when you try to use it to explain what a pulse does (Williamson shows the picture has to “magically” reassemble itself in a way that doesn’t correspond to any real physical process).
The uniform model. This is the one Williamson argues for. A spin can point in any direction on a sphere, with no restriction to two special cones. In the absence of a field, spin orientations are scattered uniformly over the whole sphere. Turn on the field, and nothing snaps into place — instead, each spin starts precessing around the field direction, and very gradually, the population of orientations becomes slightly denser near the “north pole” (aligned with the field) than near the south pole. That slight density skew, averaged over an enormous number of spins, is the macroscopic magnetization we measure. Nothing here requires quantum discreteness — it’s exactly the picture of a swarm of tiny gyroscopes precessing around a field, with a slow drift toward alignment layered on top.
The payoff of the uniform model, according to Williamson, is that it’s the only one of the three that gives a coherent, contradiction-free account of all three basic scenarios: equilibrium, the effect of a 90° pulse, and relaxation.






Figure 1: Three ways to draw an ensemble of nuclear spins at equilibrium — original schematic redrawings inspired by Williamson’s Figs. 1–3 and Hanson’s Figs. 1–3, not reproductions.

title: Why Spins Relax
section: Hanson’s classical MR — and the same picture, from a different door
text:
Hanson’s classical MR — and the same picture, from a different door
Hanson’s paper arrives at essentially the same destination — a “spins pointing everywhere, precessing, slightly skewed toward the field” picture — but he gets there by attacking three specific myths he thinks distort how MR is taught:

Myth 1: that an MR measurement forces individual protons into the “spin up” or “spin down” eigenstate. He argues this conflates a single-particle Stern-Gerlach-style measurement (which really does force a collapse) with what an MR scanner actually does (measure the bulk magnetization of trillions of spins at once, a much gentler kind of measurement that doesn’t collapse individual spins at all).
Myth 2: that MR itself is “a quantum effect.” He agrees the proton’s spin is a quantum property, but argues the behavior of MR — precession, resonance, pulses — is accurately described by classical mechanics, full stop, and doesn’t need quantum reasoning to be understood.
Myth 3: that an RF pulse works by “bringing spins into phase.” He shows this is inconsistent with the physics: a uniform RF field can only rotate the whole distribution of spins rigidly, it can never selectively rearrange spins relative to each other.

The physical picture Hanson lands on — spins scattered over a sphere, precessing, biased slightly toward the field by relaxation — is essentially identical to Williamson’s uniform model, arrived at independently and for slightly different pedagogical reasons.
Hanson’s strongest piece of support for “MR is classical” is a genuinely striking mathematical fact, due to Feynman, Vernon, and Hellwarth (1957): for an isolated two-level quantum system (like a single spin) sitting in an external field, the Schrödinger equation can be rewritten exactly as a classical vector precessing under a torque — the same equation that governs a classical bar magnet. This isn’t an approximation or a loose analogy; for this specific problem (a closed system, no environment, no dissipation), quantum and classical descriptions are mathematically the same object viewed two ways.

title: Why Spins Relax
section: Where classical physics genuinely earns its keep
text:
Where classical physics genuinely earns its keep
Putting the two papers together, classical mechanics correctly and exactly handles:

Precession: a spin in a field behaves like a gyroscope, precessing at a fixed rate (the Larmor frequency) around the field axis. No quantum reasoning needed — this is the Feynman-Vernon-Hellwarth correspondence at work.
Pulses and resonance: an RF pulse tilts the whole distribution of spins by a controllable angle, exactly like a classical torque applied on-resonance. Off-resonance behavior, flip angles, the rotating frame — all classical.
Coherence: the “bunching up” of spin phases that produces a detectable transverse signal is just a statement about the spins’ relative orientations after a pulse, not a mysterious quantum phenomenon.
The size of the equilibrium magnetization, in the regime relevant to ordinary liquid-state NMR. Hanson shows that if you take a classical magnetic dipole, assume it’s sitting in thermal equilibrium with a bath at temperature T, and apply ordinary classical statistical mechanics (the same theory Langevin used for paramagnetism in 1905, well before quantum mechanics existed), you get the exact same formula for the net magnetization as the full quantum calculation, in the weak-field/high-temperature limit relevant to real samples. The discreteness of the spin’s energy levels turns out not to matter at all in this regime — both calculations are really just leaning on ordinary Boltzmann statistics.

So: a very large fraction of “how NMR works” is legitimately classical, not just classical-flavored. This is the genuinely useful contribution both papers make — they push back against the common but misleading habit of reaching for spooky quantum language (“the spin is in superposition,” “measurement collapses the wavefunction,” “spins flip between eigenstates”) to explain phenomena that don’t need it and are actually clarified by dropping it.

title: Why Spins Relax
section: The one place this breaks: relaxation
text:
The one place this breaks: relaxation
Both papers flag relaxation — the process that brings a disturbed spin population back to equilibrium — as different. Hanson states it directly:

“Relaxation is consistent with classical mechanics, [but] the observed sizes of relaxation rates are not. Only if these are calculated based on quantum mechanics do they match experiment.” — Hanson (2008)

Williamson’s version of the mechanism (which is the one worth dwelling on, because it’s a nice physical picture) is this: a spin doesn’t relax through some abrupt “flip” from one orientation to another. Instead, a nearby atomic nucleus is also a tiny magnet, and because the surrounding molecule is constantly tumbling (ordinary thermal motion), that neighbor’s magnetic field, as felt at the location of our spin, is constantly fluctuating. Whenever that fluctuation happens to contain a component rotating at exactly the right frequency (the Larmor frequency), it acts like a very weak, very brief pulse, nudging the spin’s orientation by a tiny amount. Relaxation is the accumulation of an enormous number of these tiny, essentially random nudges.
Here’s the natural question this raises, and it’s the one that sparked the rest of this discussion: each individual nudge, considered on its own, has no reason to prefer pushing the spin toward the field over pushing it away — the neighbor’s tumbling doesn’t “know” or “care” which direction the field points. So where does the net, population-wide bias toward alignment actually come from?

title: Why Spins Relax
section: Why the bias isn’t a matter of geometry
text:
Why the bias isn’t a matter of geometry
It’s tempting to think the answer must be geometric — something about the shape of the dipole’s magnetic field, or the specific angle of approach, that somehow favors one direction. It doesn’t. If you actually simulate a classical bar-magnet-like spin, kicked only by isotropic, unbiased noise from a tumbling neighbor, with a perfectly reversible (non-dissipative) equation of motion, what you get is diffusion, not drift: the spin’s orientation randomizes across the whole sphere, with zero net polarization at the end — not the small, real, field-aligned excess we actually observe.
This is the same lesson as a classical spinning top slowly toppling over on a tabletop, and it’s worth spelling out because it clarifies what’s really doing the work. A top doesn’t fall because gravity somehow “wins an argument” against its spin — a frictionless top would precess forever at a fixed tilt. It falls because friction and air drag are draining its rotational energy, and friction is a special kind of force: by definition, it always opposes motion, so it can only ever remove energy, never add it. That directional bias is built into the force law itself, not into the geometry of the top.






Figure 2: Why a spinning top’s axis droops — friction drains rotational energy, weakening the gyroscopic stability that held the axis up. An original illustration of the analogy discussed, not a figure from either paper.



The same structure shows up if you think about a gas that’s denser on one side of a box than the other. Any individual molecular collision is completely reversible and undirected — nothing about physics says a collision has to send a molecule toward the sparse side. But there are simply more molecules launching from the dense side per second, purely because there are more of them there, so the net flow still runs from dense to sparse. The bias lives in the populations feeding the collisions, not in the collisions themselves.






Figure 3: A symmetric interaction can still produce a net, one-way drift, if the population feeding it is uneven — an original illustration, not a figure from either paper.



Nuclear spin relaxation turns out to work exactly like the gas example, not the top. The dipole-dipole “kick” connecting a spin to its neighbor is, in fact, symmetric — the same coupling strength operates whether the neighbor is about to give the spin energy or take energy away from it. What’s not symmetric is how often the neighbor happens to be caught in the configuration needed to supply that kick in each direction. A thermally-equilibrated molecular motion, like anything else at a finite temperature, spends more of its time in its own low-energy configurations than its high-energy ones. So the “spin gains a little energy” kick, which requires the neighbor to already be sitting in an unusually excited state, draws from a rarer pool than the “spin loses a little energy” kick, which just requires the neighbor’s ordinary, common low-energy motion. Multiply a symmetric coupling by an asymmetric population, and you get a net drift — toward lower energy, i.e., toward alignment with the field.






Figure 4: Where the bias actually lives: a symmetric coupling, riding on an asymmetric (Boltzmann-weighted) population of bath states — an original illustration of the detailed-balance argument.

title: Why Spins Relax
section: Why this specific asymmetry needs quantum mechanics
text:
Why this specific asymmetry needs quantum mechanics
Here’s the sting in the tail, and it’s the part that genuinely can’t be gotten around classically. The argument in Section 6 — “the bath’s own populations are unevenly distributed across its energy levels, low more common than high” — sounds like ordinary classical thermodynamics, and in one sense it is. But if you try to build a fully classical model of it — literally treating the nuclear spin as a classical bar magnet, obeying the same reversible torque law that makes Feynman-Vernon-Hellwarth work so beautifully for precession, driven by a classical (real-valued) random field from the tumbling neighbor — the calculation shows that classical randomness alone cannot supply the needed asymmetry. A classical noise process, evaluated forward or backward in time, looks statistically identical; there’s no way to distinguish “giving energy” from “taking energy” in its statistics. Run that kind of noise through a reversible classical equation of motion and you get pure, unbiased diffusion — exactly the “spreads out to zero polarization” result from Section 6, not the correct, observed, field-aligned equilibrium.
What breaks the tie is a genuinely quantum feature of thermal noise. Quantum mechanically, the fluctuating field from the bath is built out of mathematical objects (operators) that don’t commute — loosely, “field now, then field later” isn’t quite the same calculation as “field later, then field now,” in a way that has no classical counterpart. This asymmetry is precisely what makes a quantum thermal bath able to absorb a small packet of energy more readily than it can spontaneously supply one, and the size of that imbalance is set exactly by the Boltzmann factor — the same exponential that governs ordinary thermal populations, but now controlling the rate of transitions rather than just their eventual population ratio. It’s this same feature, incidentally, that explains why a lightbulb filament’s atoms spontaneously emit light more readily than they spontaneously absorb it from a cooler room — a closely related phenomenon (Einstein’s A and B coefficients) with the same underlying cause.
The historical footnote here is almost too neat: the very paper Hanson cites for “quantum two-level dynamics equals classical MR” — Feynman, Vernon, and Hellwarth, 1957 — is about a spin with no environment at all: just the spin and an external field, a closed system. That’s exactly the regime where the classical correspondence is exact. Feynman and Vernon (without Hellwarth) went on, in 1963, to write the paper that essentially founded the modern theory of how a quantum system exchanges energy with a dissipative environment — a completely different and much harder problem. It’s in that second body of work, not the first, that the quantum/classical split over relaxation actually lives.

title: Why Spins Relax
section: Reconciling this with Hanson’s equilibrium-magnetization calculation
text:
Reconciling this with Hanson’s equilibrium-magnetization calculation
At first glance, Hanson’s own result — that a purely classical statistical-mechanics calculation gives the same equilibrium magnetization as the quantum one — can look like it contradicts everything in Section 7. It doesn’t, once you notice what kind of calculation it is. Hanson’s derivation assumes the spin has already reached thermal equilibrium with the bath, then asks what that equilibrium looks like. It’s a statement about the destination, not the journey. It’s true, and it’s a nice result, but it deliberately sidesteps the dynamical question of whether the physical kicking-around process (dipole-dipole nudges from a tumbling neighbor) is actually what gets a spin to that destination, and at what rate, and in the right direction. That dynamical question is exactly where his own, separate remark applies: the qualitative mechanism is classical, but the actual rates — which encode the direction and speed of the approach to equilibrium — need quantum mechanics to come out right. Even his own tumble-dryer analogy for relaxation, if you look closely, quietly relies on real mechanical friction between the compasses and the dryer drum — genuine dissipation, not a purely conservative magnetic interaction — which is exactly the missing ingredient identified in Section 7.

title: Why Spins Relax
text:
The takeaway
There’s a clean division of labor buried in all of this, and it’s a genuinely satisfying place to land:
Classical mechanics — ordinary vectors, torques, and even ordinary classical statistical mechanics — correctly handles anything that’s either (a) reversible, closed-system dynamics (precession, pulses, coherence — the Feynman-Vernon-Hellwarth regime), or (b) a pure equilibrium calculation that doesn’t ask how the system got there (the size of the net magnetization, in the classical limit). This covers the overwhelming majority of what a working understanding of NMR/MRI actually requires, and both Williamson and Hanson deserve credit for showing that clearly and for identifying exactly which textbook habits (forced eigenstates, “spin flips,” RF pulses “bringing spins into phase”) are artifacts of reaching for quantum language where it isn’t earning its keep.
What classical mechanics cannot supply, no matter how you draw the geometry, is the actual mechanism that drives an out-of-equilibrium spin population toward the correct thermal equilibrium — the reason the drift exists at all, which direction it runs, and (quantitatively) how fast it happens. That’s not a defect in the geometric picture; it’s a real, specific, identifiable gap, and it comes from the fact that quantum thermal noise is subtly but fundamentally different from classical thermal noise. Relaxation — T1 — is where the “just draw a classical vector” strategy runs out of road, and it runs out for a genuinely interesting reason rather than an arbitrary one.






Figure 5: T1 recovery: the slow, statistically-biased drift back to equilibrium alignment. This is the shape of curve produced by the mechanism in the preceding sections, and it’s the physical property behind T1-weighted MRI contrast.



For what it’s worth: this is also exactly why T1 is useful in MRI. It’s a real physical property that differs between tissues — how efficiently a given tissue’s molecular environment can accept energy back from the spins — and that difference in relaxation rate, not the coherent precession physics, is what produces T1-weighted contrast between gray matter, white matter, and CSF.

title: Why Spins Relax
section: Seeing it run: the Spins2Bulk repository
text:
Seeing it run: the Spins2Bulk repository
Everything above has a working implementation close at hand: the Spins2Bulk MATLAB code, which simulates individual spins as vectors and shows the bulk magnetization emerge as their sum — the uniform model, built as running code rather than a static figure. It cites the same two papers this whole summary is built from, and its own teaching notes describe it as written for “an fMRI course aimed at early stage PhD students in cognitive neuroscience with limited physics background” — close enough to this document’s audience that it seemed worth actually running it rather than just describing it. Base MATLAB isn’t available here, but the code turned out to run without modification under GNU Octave, so the three figures below are genuine output from the repository’s own functions, not recreations.
The uniform model itself. boltzmannDistribution.m builds the elevation density directly from the physics in Section 2: its probability density is proportional to exp(k·sin θ)·|cos θ|, which is exactly exp(−E/kT) with the spin’s energy E = −μB₀sin θ, times a geometric factor for how much of the sphere’s surface sits at each elevation. k bundles together μB₀/kT and is deliberately exaggerated — real k at 3 T and body temperature is about 3×10⁻⁵, some 100,000 times smaller than the k = 3 used for display — for exactly the reason Williamson’s own numbers illustrate in Section 2: the true bias is far too small to draw. Running the function directly reproduces the repository’s own tutorial figure:






Figure 6: Genuine output of boltzmannDistribution.m (run via Octave), reproducing tutorial1_equilibrium.m’s own figure. At k = 3, 95.3% of spins have positive elevation and the Langevin equilibrium Mz per spin is 0.672 — both far larger than the real, physical bias.



The code’s own tutorial then computes that real bias explicitly, independent of anything in this document: at 3 T and 310 K it gets a polarization of about 9.9×10⁻⁶, or roughly 1 spin in 101,000 — the same order of magnitude as Williamson’s own worked example (about 1 in 12,000, at his higher field of 11.4 T), computed a completely different way. Seeing two independent calculations land in the same regime is a reasonable check that Section 2’s account of the bias is right.
T1 as detailed balance, made literal. relaxationLongitudinal.m is the most direct connection to Sections 6–7. At each time step, a spin’s elevation is nudged up or down by a small fixed amount, and the probability of nudging up rather than down is set to B.pdf(θ+dx) / (B.pdf(θ+dx) + B.pdf(θ−dx)) — literally the ratio of the target equilibrium density at the two candidate elevations. That is a textbook Metropolis/Glauber sampler: a symmetric-looking local step whose acceptance probabilities are weighted by the target distribution, which is mathematically guaranteed to converge to that distribution regardless of where the population starts. It is, in other words, an executable version of Figure 4 — a step that looks even-handed, riding on an asymmetric weighting that forces a net drift toward equilibrium.
It’s worth being precise about what this does and doesn’t demonstrate, in the spirit of Section 7. The code doesn’t simulate a physical dipole-dipole interaction or an explicit bath — it starts from the known target distribution and builds a sampler engineered to reach it. That’s a faithful and honest picture of what detailed balance accomplishes once you have it (Section 6), but it doesn’t, by construction, show where nature’s own asymmetry between “up” and “down” actually comes from (Section 7’s quantum argument) — that ingredient is supplied here by design, not derived. Running simulateSpins.m with the repository’s own defaults (a 90° pulse applied to the equilibrium distribution, T1 = 0.8 s) and fitting a single exponential to the recovery gives a measured T1 of 0.80 s — matching the requested value, and matching the accuracy the README itself claims for this exact preparation:






Figure 7: Genuine output of simulateSpins.m (run via Octave): Mz(t) recovering after a 90° pulse. A single-exponential fit to this run gives T1 = 0.80 s against a requested 0.80 s.



Reversible versus irreversible dephasing. The repository also includes a spin echo demonstration, which is a T2 analogue of the same reversible/irreversible distinction that separates Feynman-Vernon-Hellwarth’s closed, coherent dynamics (Section 3) from genuine relaxation (Sections 6–7) — worth showing even though it’s T2, not T1. A spread of static field offsets across spins causes fast, but reversible, dephasing (T2∗): a 180° pulse flips the fan of phases over and it re-converges into an echo. The random-walk dephasing underneath it, true T2, is not reversible, so the echo is capped at exp(−TE/T2) rather than exp(−TE/T2∗):






Figure 8: Genuine output of simulateSpins.m (run via Octave): free decay at \(T_2^*\) ≈ 9 ms (red) versus a spin echo (blue) from the same \(T_2\) = 200 ms population. The echo re-forms near the predicted t = 42 ms, tracking the exp(−t/T2) envelope rather than the much faster \(T_2^*\) decay.



For anyone who wants to go further than these three figures, the repository’s tutorials/tutorial1_equilibrium.m walks through exactly the Section 2/4 material as a runnable MATLAB Live Script, and s_SpinsToBulkM.m has worked cells for precession, pulses, T1, T2, T2∗, the spin echo, and a BOLD-contrast demonstration that extends the T1-weighting point in the footnote above to T2∗-weighting — directly relevant groundwork for an fMRI course.
Sources: Williamson, M.P. “Drawing Single NMR Spins and Understanding Relaxation,” Natural Product Communications, May 2019 (DOI: 10.1177/1934578X19849790). Hanson, L.G. “Is Quantum Mechanics Necessary for Understanding Magnetic Resonance?” Concepts in Magnetic Resonance Part A, 2008. Spins2Bulk (MATLAB code), subroutines boltzmannDistribution.m, relaxationLongitudinal.m, relaxationTransverse.m and simulateSpins.m. Figures 1-5 are original schematic illustrations created to convey the same concepts as figures in the two papers above; they are not reproductions. Figures 6-8 are genuine output of the Spins2Bulk code, run unmodified under GNU Octave.

title: Felix Bloch and the Bloch Equations
text:
The Bloch Equations
For the longitudinal component and the magnitude of transverse magnetization, the relaxation part of the Bloch equations describes recovery and decay after RF excitation:
\[
M_z(t) = M_0\left(1 - e^{-t/T_1}\right)
\]
\[
M_{xy}(t) = M_{xy}(0)e^{-t/T_2}
\]
Here, \(M_0\) is the equilibrium magnetization, \(T_1\) is the longitudinal relaxation time, and \(T_2\) is the transverse relaxation time. For an ideal \(90^\circ\) pulse, \(M_{xy}(0) = M_0\).
crumbs: Felix Bloch and the Bloch Equations

title: Felix Bloch and the Bloch Equations
text:
Differential Equation Form

The same relaxation processes can be written as ordinary differential equations:
\[
\frac{dM_z}{dt} = \frac{M_0 - M_z}{T_1}
\]
\[
\frac{dM_{xy}}{dt} = -\frac{M_{xy}}{T_2}
\]
The first equation returns \(M_z\) toward its equilibrium value; the second causes \(M_{xy}\) to decay toward zero. They are ordinary differential equations because they describe changes with time at one location. Spatially varying fields and diffusion add further terms later in the course.
crumbs: Felix Bloch and the Bloch Equations

title: Felix Bloch and the Bloch Equations
text:
About Felix Bloch



Felix Bloch at Stanford


Felix Bloch was born in Zurich on 23 October 1905 to the Jewish businessman Gustav Bloch and his wife Agnes.
After leaving school, he embarked on a degree in engineering at ETH Zurich in 1924 before switching to the Department of Mathematics and Physics one year later. At a time of his degree, important groundwork was being laid for quantum physics in Zurich. As a student, he attended lectures by Peter Debye, Paul Scherrer and Hermann Weyl, and seminars by Erwin Schrödinger, who was researching wave mechanics at the University of Zurich’s Physics Institute and showcased his famous wave equation for the hydrogen atom for the first time in 1926.
crumbs: Felix Bloch and the Bloch Equations

title: Felix Bloch and the Bloch Equations
text:
Doctorate and years as assistant
In November 1927 Bloch moved to the University of Leipzig and, at the age of 22, began a dissertation under Werner Heisenberg, who was only four years his senior and whom he soon befriended. As Heisenberg’s first doctoral student, he followed his advice and studied the movement of electrons in periodical lattice potential and the resulting conductivity in his thesis entitled “Über die Quantenmechanik der Elektronen in Kristallgittern”, thereby paving the way for his subsequent fame. After completing his doctorate, he returned to ETH Zurich for a year at the end of 1928 as an assistant to Wolfgang Pauli before taking up assistantships under Adriaan Fokker and Hendrik A. Kramers in Holland. In 1930 Bloch returned to the University of Leipzig as a senior assistant of Heisenberg’s, where he became a professor the following year with his paper “Zur Theorie des Austauschproblems und der Remanenzerscheinung der Ferromagnetica”. In the meantime, he also conducted research at Niels Bohr’s institute in Copenhagen.
crumbs: Felix Bloch and the Bloch Equations

title: Felix Bloch and the Bloch Equations
text:
Emigration to the USA
The seizure of power by the Nazis and especially the “Gesetz zur Wiederherstellung des Berufsbeamtentums” (Civil Service Restoration Act) passed in April 1933 put an abrupt end to the collaboration between Bloch and Heisenberg. The strict implementation of the law by the education ministry responsible forced Bloch to abandon his position as a physicist at the University of Leipzig against his and Heisenberg’s will in May 1933 and leave Germany for Switzerland. A few months later, he left Europe altogether and emigrated to the USA in 1934 to take up a professorship at Stanford University. The change in continent was also mirrored by a scientific change of tack. He began to move away from his more theoretical focus and increasingly towards experimental physics. His research primarily concentrated on the magnetism of atomic cores and their components, protons and – only discovered in 1932 – neutrons.
crumbs: Felix Bloch and the Bloch Equations
