It was not until the arrival of Swiss physicist Felix Bloch, however, in 1934, that physics research at Stanford truly caught fire. A refugee from the Nazis, Bloch was only 28 years old when he answered David Webster’s invitation to join the Stanford faculty. …
Soon after he arrived at Stanford, Bloch, together with Berkeley physicist Robert Oppenheimer, organized a joint seminar on theoretical physics that met alternately at Stanford and Berkeley. Many of the leading physicists of Europe and the United States traveled to the West Coast to speak at these seminars, and many came to Stanford as summer visitors. By the mid-1930s, Stanford was recognized as an important center for physics, despite the fact that geographically it was considered far removed from the center of “civilization!”

title: Erwin L. Hahn and the Spin Echo
text:
The Original Spin-Echo Paper
Hahn’s paper, Spin Echoes, appeared in Physical Review in 1950. It showed how timed RF pulses can create an observable echo and use its decay to measure relaxation. This is the text from Hahn’s 1950 paper introducing the idea of Spin Echos.
Notice how much you have learned in the first few weeks. It should be largely comprehensible, although the language may seem a bit old-fashioned.
crumbs: Erwin L. Hahn and the Spin Echo

title: Erwin L. Hahn and the Spin Echo
text:
ABSTRACT Intense radio frequency power in the form of pulses is applied to an ensemble of spins in a liquid placed in a large static magnetic field H0. The frequency of the pulsed r-f power satisfies the condition for nuclear magnetic resonance, and the pulses last for times which are short compared with the time in which the nutating macroscopic magnetic moment of the entire spin ensemble can decay. After removal of the pulses a non-equilibrium configuration of isochromatic macroscopic moments remains in which the moment vectors precess freely. Each moment vector has a magnitude at a given precession frequency which is determined by the distribution of Larmor frequencies imposed upon the ensemble by inhomogeneities in H0.


At times determined by pulse sequences applied in the past the constructive interference of these moment vectors gives rise to observable spontaneous nuclear induction signals. The properties and underlying principles of these spin echo signals are discussed with use of the Bloch theory.


Relaxation times are measured directly and accurately from the measurement of echo amplitudes. An analysis includes the effect on relaxation measurements of the self-diffusion of liquid molecules which contain resonant nuclei. Preliminary studies are made of several effects associated with spin echoes, including the observed shifts in magnetic resonance frequency of spins due to magnetic shielding of nuclei contained in molecules.
crumbs: Erwin L. Hahn and the Spin Echo

title: Erwin L. Hahn and the Spin Echo
text:
Hahn at Berkeley
The biographical record describes Hahn’s long career at the University of California, Berkeley and his recognition for the development of pulsed magnetic resonance and signal refocusing.
He was professor of physics, from 1955 to 1991, and subsequently, Professor Emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. … In 2013, Sir Peter Mansfield said in his autobiography that Hahn was “the person who really missed out” the Nobel Prize for his contribution to the principles of spin echoes.[6] He also received the 2016 Gold Medal from the International Society for Magnetic Resonance in Medicine (ISMRM). The award, ISMRM’s highest honor, was given to Hahn for his creation of pulsed magnetic resonance and processes of signal refocusing which are essential to modern day MRI.[7]
crumbs: Erwin L. Hahn and the Spin Echo

title: Erwin L. Hahn and the Spin Echo
text:
Hahn’s Stanford Connection

Hahn recalled that a National Research Council fellowship brought him to Stanford, where he worked with Felix Bloch and continued his work on spin echoes. The connection links the history of the spin echo to the development of the Bloch equations.

… but that’s how I got one of the National Research Council Fellowships. So with that in my bonnet, Nordsieck, who was there at Illinois, had of course previously worked with Felix Bloch. They’d done some theory together. He said, “Why don’t you go to Stanford? Bloch is a good man and you’d learn a lot.” So I said, “OK,” and California attracted me, since I’d been there during the war in the Navy in training school, so I went to Stanford and that’s how I became a post-doc for one year, a fellow, and then I was an instructor for one year. So there I continued my work on spin echoes and directed a student of his, under me as well, a PhD, and we did a problem together.

title: Fast Exchange Model
text:
T1 from multiple molecules
A voxel can contain water in several environments at once: bulk free water, water near a molecular surface, and water more tightly associated with a molecule. In this simple model, surface-associated water has a shorter \(T_1\) than bulk water.
If water molecules exchange between these environments quickly compared with the relaxation process—the fast-exchange assumption—the voxel does not show a mixture of separate exponentials. Instead, it shows a single exponential recovery whose rate is the concentration-weighted average of the individual rates:
\[
\frac{1}{T_1(L)} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} C_i \frac{1}{T_{1,c_i}} + \left(1 - \sum_{i=1}^{n} C_i\right)\frac{1}{T_{1,f}}
\]
Here, \(C_i\) is the fraction of water in environment \(i\), and the remaining fraction is bulk free water. Notice that it is the rates that average, not the time constants. This is the same bookkeeping that appears in the next chapter, where the rates of two dephasing mechanisms add to give \(T_2^*\). Fast exchange is a useful starting model for understanding why a voxel with several water environments can have one apparent \(T_1\); related models are used in quantitative \(T_1\) methods later in the book.
Fast exchange does not apply in every situation. If exchange is slow, the recovery can contain more than one exponential and a more detailed model is needed. Still, fast exchange is a good starting place for many analyses—and discovering where it fails can be scientifically useful.

section: The importance of the Fourier Series
text:
The importance of the Fourier Series
The Wikipedia page summarizes Fourier’s contributions this way. I think they might not be generous enough.

Fourier’s Claim: Joseph Fourier asserted that any function (continuous or discontinuous) can be written as an infinite sum of sine waves.
The Conceptual Breakthrough: While his claim was overbroad without boundary conditions, recognizing that infinite series could represent discontinuous functions - like a step function or an impulse - was a major mathematical leap.
Lagrange vs. Dirichlet: Lagrange had previously solved specific instances; he assumed the technique generalized, but never proved it. Dirichlet later provided the first rigorous proof of convergence under explicit, restrictive conditions.
The Legacy: Resolving when these series converge drove fundamental developments in real analysis for over a century and laid the groundwork for the modern Fourier transform.

title: Phineas Gage
text:
The Accident and Its Aftermath
Gage was 25 years old, tamping gunpowder into a hole drilled in rock, when the charge detonated prematurely and drove the iron rod through his left cheek, behind his eye, and out through the top of his skull. He was not killed, and remarkably his sight and speech were largely spared. His skull, and the tamping iron itself, are preserved at the Warren Anatomical Museum at Harvard Medical School.
The account of Gage’s altered personality comes primarily from his attending physician, John Martyn Harlow, who described a dramatic change:
Gage’s subsequent life was difficult. He was rejected by his former employers as unfit for work, and for a time he drifted around the United States and South America, exhibiting himself and the tamping iron that had deformed his skull.

title: Phineas Gage
text:
Figure 2: The skull of Phineas Gage, the object most subsequent reconstructions of his injury have relied on.





“His physical health is good, … the equilibrium or balance, so to speak, between his intellectual faculties and animal propensities seem to have been destroyed. He is fitful, irreverent, indulging at times in the grossest profanity (which was no previously his custom), manifesting but little deference for his fellows, impatient of restraint or advice when it conflicts with his desires…”


“In this regard his mind was radically changed, so decidedly that his friends and acquaintances said that he was ‘no longer Gage.’”

title: Phineas Gage
text:
Locating the Lesion
Because no autopsy was performed when Gage died in 1861, later researchers have had to reconstruct the injury from the skull itself. Damasio and colleagues used measurements from the recovered skull together with modern neuroimaging techniques to estimate the trajectory of the rod and the likely extent of damage to the frontal lobes (Damasio et al., 1994).






Figure 3: Reconstructions of the tamping iron’s trajectory through Gage’s skull, based on the physical skull and CT imaging.



A later reanalysis by Ratiu and colleagues (2004, “The Tale of Phineas Gage, Digitally Remastered”) used three-dimensional reconstruction from thin-slice CT scanning of the skull to refine this picture. Their conclusion was more conservative about the extent of injury:

“Our results show that the cerebral injury was limited to the left frontal lobe, did not extend to the contralateral side, did not affect the ventricular system, and did not involve vital intracranial vascular structures.”







Figure 4: Three-dimensional CT-based reconstruction of Gage’s skull and estimated lesion extent (Ratiu et al., 2004).

title: Phineas Gage
section: How Much of the Story Is Reliable?
text:
How Much of the Story Is Reliable?
Malcolm Macmillan, whose scholarship on Gage is the standard reference on the case, has argued that much of the well-known narrative is less certain than textbooks suggest. Writing on the 150th anniversary of the accident, he found that although Gage is mentioned in roughly 60% of introductory psychology textbooks, a great deal of what is written about him is inaccurate (Macmillan, 2000).
Several of Macmillan’s points are worth keeping in mind:

The dramatic personality description comes largely from a single later report by Harlow, not from independent contemporaneous observers. Earlier accounts were less dramatic and less detailed.
The exact trajectory of the tamping iron was never documented precisely enough to know which brain areas were destroyed. Modern reconstructions are educated estimates, not certainties.
After his recovery, Gage worked for several years as a stagecoach driver in Chile — a job that required planning, reliability, and social interaction. His behavior likely changed, but probably not to the catastrophic degree often claimed.

Macmillan’s conclusion is that Gage’s case is consistent with frontal lobe involvement in personality and decision-making, but it does not provide a simple or decisive demonstration of that link. The take-home point is not that brain injury produces a dramatic moral collapse, but that it can alter personality in ways that are real, if less tidy than the popular story suggests.

title: Phineas Gage
text:
Modern Gage-Like Cases
Cases of severe frontal or penetrating head injury with unexpectedly preserved function continue to appear in the clinical literature, and they are often explicitly compared to Gage.
Luo and Fei describe a 47-year-old man who fell from a 4-meter construction scaffold with a twisted steel bar penetrating his head (Luo & Fei, 2015). Despite the severity of the injury, and aside from the loss of vision in one eye, he recovered without major neurological sequelae.






Figure 5: A modern penetrating head injury case, compared explicitly to Phineas Gage: a twisted steel bar and the resulting CT imaging (Luo & Fei, 2015).



A separate case reported in the Lancet, “Brain of a White-Collar Worker,” describes a 44-year-old civil servant found on neuropsychological testing to have below-average IQ and massive ventricular enlargement dating back to a childhood shunt for hydrocephalus — yet with an entirely normal work and family life (Feuillet et al., 2007).






Figure 6: Massive ventricular enlargement in a patient with normal social functioning: CT and T1/T2-weighted MRI (Feuillet et al., 2007).



Taken together, these cases echo the broader lesson of Gage: the relationship between brain structure and behavior is real, but the brain’s capacity for adaptation means that structural damage alone is a poor predictor of the outcome for any one individual.





Damasio, H., Grabowski, T., Frank, R., Galaburda, A. M., & Damasio, A. R. (1994). The return of Phineas Gage: Clues about the brain from the skull of a famous patient. Science, 264(5162), 1102–1105.


Feuillet, L., Dufour, H., & Pelletier, J. (2007). Brain of a white-collar worker. Lancet (London, England), 370(9583), 262.


Luo, P., & Fei, Z. (2015). Twisted steel-induced penetrating head injury. Neurology, 84(18), 1909.


Macmillan, M. (2000). Restoring phineas gage: A 150th retrospective. Journal of The History of The Neurosciences.

title: Leukoencephalopathy and White Matter Adaptability
text:
The Case
A 66-year-old right-handed man with a history of type 2 diabetes was rear-ended by a truck, resulting in significant back and neck discomfort that brought him to the emergency department. Before the accident, he had been fully functional in all activities of daily living and was operating his own business. He had no known perinatal injury or developmental difficulties as a child, and he had graduated from high school.
His neurologic exam was notable for difficulty following multistep commands, ocular motor apraxia, and simultagnosia, but he had normal strength and coordination, with a relatively normal gait aside from a stooped posture.
CT imaging obtained in the emergency department revealed diffuse white matter changes, prompting follow-up MRI. The MRI showed prominent white matter volume loss and cavitary lesions consistent with dysmyelination or diffuse cystic leukodystrophy — with notable relative preservation of the cerebral cortex and deep gray nuclei.

title: Leukoencephalopathy and White Matter Adaptability
text: Figure 1: Sagittal and coronal T2-weighted MRI showing diffuse white matter volume loss and cavitary lesions consistent with dysmyelination or diffuse cystic leukodystrophy; axial and coronal CT from the initial presentation showing the same chronic-appearing white matter changes (Neth & Carabenciov, 2021).

title: Leukoencephalopathy and White Matter Adaptability
text:
Adaptability Despite Severe Imaging Findings
Despite the severity of these imaging findings, the patient continued to live a fully functional life. The authors present this case as clinical evidence of the remarkable adaptability of the human brain to insult — a theme that recurs throughout this set of resources, from Phineas Gage to the “Brain of a White-Collar Worker” case. In each instance, the degree of structural damage visible on imaging is a poor guide to the degree of functional impairment actually observed.





Neth, B. J., & Carabenciov, I. D. (2021). Severe adulthood leukoencephalopathy: Highlighting brain adaptability to insult. Canadian Journal of Neurological Sciences, 48(4), 585–586.

title: Developmental Hemispherectomy and Plasticity
text:
Work in Progress



Suggestions of all kinds for these lecture notes are welcome — whether it’s fixing small errors, raising bigger questions, or offering new perspectives. Please share comments through GitHub Issues. To make feedback easier to address, please point to the section you have in mind — by section number or a short snippet of text.


Hemispherectomy — surgical removal or disconnection of an entire cerebral hemisphere, most often to control severe, otherwise-intractable childhood epilepsy — is one of the most dramatic demonstrations of the developing brain’s capacity for reorganization. Children who undergo the procedure early in life can go on to recover language, motor, and cognitive function to a degree that would be impossible after equivalent damage in an adult, illustrating how much more plastic the young brain is than the mature one.
The slide below is a link to a television news segment on a case of developmental hemispherectomy. There are various things you might notice about the young girl who underwent the procedure. Have a look, and we can discuss in class.

title: The Wada Test and Its Replacement by fMRI
text:
An Invasive, Historically Important Test
The source slide embeds a video of Juhn Wada himself describing the procedure he developed:
Because it requires arterial catheterization and a brief pharmacological hemispherectomy, the Wada test is invasive, resource-intensive, and not without risk. As noninvasive functional imaging matured, it became a natural candidate to replace or supplement the Wada test for language lateralization.
crumbs: The Wada Test and Its Replacement by fMRI

title: The Wada Test and Its Replacement by fMRI
text:
fMRI as a Replacement
Multiple studies comparing fMRI with the classic Wada test — including work by Binder (1996) and Woermann (2003), and a large comparison by Janecek and colleagues (2013) in Epilepsia — show that language lateralization measured with fMRI agrees with the Wada test in roughly 85–95% of patients. As a result, many epilepsy centers now use fMRI first and reserve the Wada test for ambiguous cases, including centers such as the UCLA Seizure Disorder Center, the Cleveland Clinic Epilepsy Program, the Mayo Clinic Epilepsy Program, the University of California San Francisco Epilepsy Center, and Johns Hopkins.






Figure 1: Comparison of language lateralization indices (LIs) from fMRI and Wada testing in a large patient sample, illustrating the level of agreement between the two methods (Janecek et al., 2013, Epilepsia).
crumbs: The Wada Test and Its Replacement by fMRI

title: The Wada Test and Its Replacement by fMRI
text:
fMRI Predicting Post-Surgical Naming Outcome
A more direct test of whether fMRI can substitute for the Wada test is whether it predicts the actual clinical outcome patients care about — in this case, naming ability after left anterior temporal lobectomy (L-ATL), which can be complicated by confrontation naming deficits.
Sabsevitz and colleagues studied twenty-four patients undergoing L-ATL, each of whom received preoperative language mapping with fMRI, preoperative Wada testing for language dominance, and pre- and postoperative neuropsychological testing (Sabsevitz et al., 2003). fMRI laterality indices, reflecting the interhemispheric difference in activated volume between left and right homologous regions of interest, were calculated for each patient and related to Wada language dominance and naming outcome.

ResultResult, annotated








Figure 2: Preoperative fMRI temporal-lobe laterality index plotted against Boston Naming Test change score in patients undergoing left anterior temporal lobectomy (Sabsevitz et al., 2003).











Figure 3: The same relationship, with the two outcome clusters (small vs. large naming decline) highlighted (Sabsevitz et al., 2003).






Both the fMRI laterality index (\(p < 0.001\)) and the Wada test (\(p < 0.05\)) were predictive of naming outcome. fMRI showed 100% sensitivity and 73% specificity for predicting significant naming decline, and both fMRI and the Wada test were more predictive of outcome than age at seizure onset or preoperative naming performance.






For human review



The source slides label this study “Bookheimer: fMRI applied to pre-surgical planning,” but the quoted methods, results, and journal URL (n.neurology.org/content/60/11/1788) all match Sabsevitz et al. (2003, Neurology), which is cited above. Please confirm whether a separate Bookheimer study was intended here, or whether the slide title should simply be corrected.







Sabsevitz, D. S., Swanson, S. J., Hammeke, T. A., Spanaki, M. V., Possing, E. T., Morris, G. L., 3rd, Mueller, W. M., & Binder, J. R. (2003). Use of preoperative functional neuroimaging to predict language deficits from epilepsy surgery. Neurology, 60(11), 1788–1792.
crumbs: The Wada Test and Its Replacement by fMRI

title: Predicting Vulnerability to PTSD from Brain Activity
text:
An Early Longitudinal Study: Amygdala Reactivity Before Stress
An elegant natural experiment is available in Israeli military training, where combat paramedic trainees are known in advance to be headed for stressful, sometimes traumatic, experiences.
The study included 50 trainees (25 female, roughly 18 years old) beginning military service as combat paramedics, along with 12 non-military controls (6 female) who experienced no comparable stress. Participants were measured in the first week of training and again 18 months later. All of the military participants experienced one or more genuinely stressful events during that period — such as witnessing severe casualties or having to manage an injured patient — and self-reported stress increased significantly as a result.
The behavioral result raises an obvious question: given the wide variance in how much individual paramedics’ symptoms increased, can that variability be predicted in advance? The study’s answer was that it could, from amygdala activation measured before the stressful events occurred:
This scatter plot is worth examining critically. It is exactly the kind of correlational figure — a handful of points anchoring a wide range on one axis, with a linear fit drawn through them — that deserves a skeptical look at how much the fit is being driven by a few extreme points versus a genuinely graded relationship across the whole sample.
crumbs: Predicting Vulnerability to PTSD from Brain Activity

title: Predicting Vulnerability to PTSD from Brain Activity
text:
Figure 2: Study design: paramedic trainees and non-military controls were scanned and assessed at the start of training and again roughly 18 months later, after paramedics had experienced stressful events on the job.










Figure 3: PTSD Diagnostic Scale (PDS) scores before and after the stress-exposure period. Scores were low and similar across groups beforehand; scores increased afterward for the paramedics but not the age-matched controls, with a great deal of individual variability.





“Predisposition to stress vulnerability was revealed by showing that high levels of amygdala reactivity before the stressful event predicted a greater increase in stress symptoms following it.”







Figure 4: PDS increase (18-month follow-up minus baseline) plotted against amygdala activation measured before stress exposure, with a linear fit (\(r = 0.70\)).
crumbs: Predicting Vulnerability to PTSD from Brain Activity

title: Predicting Vulnerability to PTSD from Brain Activity
text:
A Modern Reassessment
A later summary judgment on this line of work is that the original amygdala-reactivity study is still respected as an early longitudinal demonstration that amygdala reactivity may predispose people to PTSD, but that subsequent research shows the picture is more complicated: vulnerability appears to depend on distributed brain networks and environmental factors rather than any single region, and fMRI measures are not yet predictive enough for practical clinical screening.






Figure 5: A more recent connectome-based predictive modeling study of PTSD development, illustrating the shift from single-region measures toward distributed network models measured at multiple post-trauma timepoints.



That study measured trauma survivors approximately 1 month post-trauma and used connectome-based predictive modeling (CPM), focused on whole-brain functional networks rather than a single region of interest, to predict PTSD severity as far out as 14 months later. Among 162 recent trauma survivors, CPM significantly predicted PTSD severity at 1 month and at 14 months post-trauma, but not at 6 months — and the networks that were most predictive differed somewhat between the 1-month and 14-month predictions, with the anterior default mode, motor-sensory, and salience networks most implicated early on, joined later by central executive and visual networks.
crumbs: Predicting Vulnerability to PTSD from Brain Activity

title: Predicting Vulnerability to PTSD from Brain Activity
section: Replication After the Boston Marathon Bombing
text:
Replication After the Boston Marathon Bombing
McLaughlin and colleagues had a rare opportunity to test the amygdala-reactivity hypothesis prospectively: they had already scanned a cohort of young adults before the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing and the manhunt and shelter-in-place order that followed it, and were able to examine whether neural function measured before the attack predicted PTSD symptom onset afterward (McLaughlin et al., 2014).

AmygdalaHippocampus








Figure 6: Amygdala activation to negative vs. neutral faces (measured before the attack) plotted against later PTSD symptoms (McLaughlin et al., 2014).











Figure 7: The corresponding relationship for hippocampal activation (McLaughlin et al., 2014).






The conclusion: heightened amygdala reactivity to negative emotional information was associated with the future onset of posttraumatic symptoms following the attack, independent of participants’ prior internalizing symptoms (including prior PTSD symptoms) and prior violence exposure. This independence from prior symptoms is what makes the finding a genuine prospective biomarker candidate rather than simply a restatement of prior vulnerability.
crumbs: Predicting Vulnerability to PTSD from Brain Activity

title: Predicting Vulnerability to PTSD from Brain Activity
text:
A Larger-Scale Follow-Up
At the time, only two studies with relatively small samples had examined this prospective association — the Israeli paramedic study above (warzone-adjacent combat training) and the McLaughlin et al. Boston Marathon study (a terrorist attack) — both finding that relatively increased amygdala reactivity measured before a major traumatic event predicted greater subsequent PTSD symptoms.
Swartz, Williamson, and Hariri addressed this with a substantially larger sample: 340 healthy young adults followed longitudinally, with amygdala reactivity to fearful and angry faces measured at baseline and internalizing symptoms tracked at regular intervals afterward (published in Neuron, 2015).






Figure 8: Individual differences in threat-related amygdala reactivity, measured at baseline, plotted against internalizing symptoms following variable amounts of subsequently reported life stress.



Individuals with relatively heightened amygdala reactivity at baseline who also went on to report greater life stress after scanning showed significantly greater symptoms at follow-up — demonstrating that amygdala reactivity predicts psychological vulnerability to life stress occurring as much as one to four years later, in a sample far larger than the earlier combat and terrorist-attack studies.
crumbs: Predicting Vulnerability to PTSD from Brain Activity

title: Predicting Vulnerability to PTSD from Brain Activity
section: Prefrontal Cortex as a Resilience Factor
text:
Prefrontal Cortex as a Resilience Factor
Most of the studies above focus on the amygdala as a vulnerability marker. A complementary line of work asks whether prefrontal activity — associated with regulating, rather than generating, emotional responses — instead predicts resilience.
Kaldewaij and colleagues followed 185 police recruits who experienced their core trauma in the line of duty, in a prospective longitudinal study (Kaldewaij et al., 2021). Before and after trauma exposure, recruits performed a well-established fMRI approach–avoidance task that maps impulsive versus controlled emotional actions.

Design and behaviorPrefrontal cortexAmygdala








Figure 9: Study design and behavioral results: recruits varied widely in how much their trauma symptoms changed from baseline to follow-up (Kaldewaij et al., 2021).











Figure 10: Anterior prefrontal cortex (aPFC) activity during emotion control, and its relationship to later symptom change (Kaldewaij et al., 2021).











Figure 11: Amygdala activation in the same cohort, shown for comparison with the prefrontal results (Kaldewaij et al., 2021).






Higher baseline activity in the anterior prefrontal cortex — dorsal and medial frontal pole regions in particular — was related to lower PTSD symptoms after trauma exposure, and aPFC activity predicted symptom development over and above self-reported and behavioral measures. Trauma exposure itself, but not the resulting trauma symptoms, predicted amygdala activation at follow-up. The authors interpret this as evidence that prefrontal emotion-regulation capacity, rather than amygdala reactivity alone, may be an important predictor of resilience against developing PTSD symptoms.
The source slides also raise a methodological caution worth preserving here explicitly: some of the reported prefrontal associations were, in the authors’ own framing, only weakly (“very slightly”) related to symptom change, and the slides flag a concern about “double-dipping” — the risk of selecting a region of interest based on the same data used to test the association, which can inflate apparent effect sizes. This is a useful point to raise with students alongside the results themselves.






For human review



This file covers slides 32–46 of the source deck. The originally requested range was slides 32–49, but the deck itself contains only 46 slides in total — the last slide (46, “Amygdala”) is the final slide of the presentation. Please confirm this is expected, or point to the correct source file if additional slides were intended.







Kaldewaij, R., Koch, S. B. J., Hashemi, M. M., Zhang, W., Klumpers, F., & Roelofs, K. (2021). Anterior prefrontal brain activity during emotion control predicts resilience to post-traumatic stress symptoms. Nature Human Behaviour, 5(8), 1055–1064.


McLaughlin, K. A., Busso, D. S., Duys, A., Green, J. G., Alves, S., Way, M., & Sheridan, M. A. (2014). Amygdala response to negative stimuli predicts PTSD symptom onset following a terrorist attack. Depression and Anxiety, 31(10), 834–842.
crumbs: Predicting Vulnerability to PTSD from Brain Activity

title: The T1w/T2w Ratio for Myelin Mapping
text:
The idea
The T1w/T2w method was introduced by Glasser and Van Essen (2011) as a way to map cortical areas from myelin content (Figure 1). In fact, they refer to the method as myelin mapping.
The idea of the method is that by taking the ratio of these two images, a space-varying bias of the MR images is eliminated. Namely, the MR receive-coil sensitivity varies as we measure across the brain volume. The excite-coil differences are less severe because excitation is typically performed by the whole body coil.
The T1-weighted and a T2-weighted images both carry a similar receive-coil intensity bias. After all, they are measured using the same coils. If we take the ratio, the receive-coil bias divides out. When measuring the white matter, the thinking goes, the biggest image contrast will be due to myelin. Thus, Glasser and Van Essen suggested that the resulting T1w/T2w maps are essentially measurements of myelin contrast.
The attractive feature of these T1w/T2w ratios (myelin maps) is the ease of their implementation. 3T scanners and pulse sequences can all make such measurements from standard sequences, without any special pulse sequence development. Support for the idea came from the observation that when these data are mapped to the cortical surface, the spatial gradients of the group map agree well with cytoarchitectonic areal borders. So the ratio became a widely used, low-cost proxy for cortical myelination. Other, more biologically based gold-standard methods exist but the measurements are difficult to make and analyze. Anyone who can divide can make this measurement.
crumbs: The T1w/T2w Ratio for Myelin Mapping

title: The T1w/T2w Ratio for Myelin Mapping
text: Figure 1: Glasser and Van Essen (2011) introduced the T1w/T2w ratio to map cortical areas by myelin content; the ratio cancels the shared receive-coil intensity bias.
crumbs: The T1w/T2w Ratio for Myelin Mapping

title: The T1w/T2w Ratio for Myelin Mapping
section: Why the ratio is not a specific myelin measure
text:
Why the ratio is not a specific myelin measure
The convenience of the method should not be mistaken for validity. A series of studies comparing the T1w/T2w ratio against histology and against more direct myelin-MRI measures — quantitative susceptibility mapping, magnetization transfer saturation, and multi-echo myelin water fraction (MWF) — find that the ratio does not track myelin specifically, especially in white matter (Figure 2, Figure 3).
Several findings recur across this literature. In the corpus callosum the T1w/T2w map does not positively correlate with Luxol-fast-blue optical density and shows, if anything, a weak negative correlation, whereas myelin water fraction correlates strongly and positively with the histology. Direct method comparisons find only weak correlations between the T1w/T2w ratio and both SyMRI relaxometry and MT saturation, even though those two agree well with each other.






Figure 2: Studies reporting a discrepancy between T1w/T2w maps and histology, and weak correlations with other myelin-MRI measures.



And reliability is not the issue — the ratio is highly reproducible test–retest — but reproducibility is not validity: a measure can be stable yet still fail to reflect the quantity of interest. The reasonable summary is that the T1w/T2w ratio may correlate with myelin at the cortical level but is not a specific map of myelin density in white matter, and should be used with that limitation in mind.






Figure 3: Test–retest and concurrent-validity comparisons: the T1w/T2w ratio is reliable but has low criterion validity as an index of myelin, particularly in white and subcortical structures.
crumbs: The T1w/T2w Ratio for Myelin Mapping

title: Brain Beats: Pulsatile Motion and Flow
text:
Amplified MRI
Cardiac-driven brain motion is small, but it can be made visible. Amplified MRI (aMRI) takes retrospectively cardiac-gated MRI data and exaggerates the tiny frame-to-frame displacements, much as Eulerian video magnification amplifies subtle motion in ordinary video. A phase-based amplification algorithm improves on the original intensity-based approach, producing a clearer, less noisy visualization of how the brain deforms over the cardiac cycle.
crumbs: Brain Beats: Pulsatile Motion and Flow

title: Brain Beats: Pulsatile Motion and Flow
text:
Video
Amplified MRI (aMRI): cardiac-driven brain motion, exaggerated for visualization.
crumbs: Brain Beats: Pulsatile Motion and Flow

title: Brain Beats: Pulsatile Motion and Flow
text:
The fluid compartments
To interpret these signals it helps to keep the brain’s fluid compartments in mind (Figure 1). By volume the brain is mostly intracellular fluid (~65%), with interstitial (extracellular) fluid (~15%), CSF (~10%), and blood (~10%) making up the rest. The blood is separated from the other compartments by the blood–brain barrier and the blood–CSF barrier, formed by tight junctions between endothelial or choroid-plexus epithelial cells. CSF is produced at the choroid plexus, circulates through the ventricles and subarachnoid spaces, and — in the glymphatic model — exchanges with interstitial fluid along perivascular routes gated by astrocytic aquaporin-4 channels.






Figure 1: The brain’s fluid compartments and barriers: ventricles and choroid plexus, the blood–brain barrier, and the blood–CSF barrier (after Jessen et al., “The Glymphatic System: A Beginner’s Guide”).
crumbs: Brain Beats: Pulsatile Motion and Flow

title: Brain Beats: Pulsatile Motion and Flow
section: Cardiac pulsations in the MR signal
text:
Cardiac pulsations in the MR signal
Functional MRI is sensitive to blood flow, oxygenation, and volume, and these change on two very different time scales (Figure 2). The familiar BOLD hemodynamic response unfolds over ~10–20 s. Superimposed on it are much faster cardiac pulsations, once per heartbeat. The clinical motivation — conditions such as migraine and raised intracranial pressure — is to build a tool that characterizes the whole-brain distribution and timing of these pulsations rapidly at 3 T.






Figure 2: Functional MRI is influenced by blood flow, oxygenation, and volume. The slow BOLD response (top) and the fast cardiac pulsations (bottom) occur on very different time scales.



Resolving pulsations that recur roughly once per second requires fast sampling and a way to reference the data to the heartbeat (Figure 3). A pulse oximeter on the thumb records the photoplethysmogram (PPG). The fMRI signal is sampled quickly (here TR = 250 ms, slice acquisition time 50 ms), each sample is aligned to the nearest heartbeat peak, and the aligned traces are averaged across many beats. Splitting the data into even and odd heartbeats and comparing the two averages gives a direct estimate of the measurement’s reliability.






Figure 3: Measuring cardiac pulsations. A thumb pulse oximeter (A) provides the heartbeat reference for the rapidly sampled fMRI signal (B); traces are aligned to heartbeat peaks (C) and averaged, with even/odd splits used to assess reliability (D).
crumbs: Brain Beats: Pulsatile Motion and Flow

title: Brain Beats: Pulsatile Motion and Flow
text:
Where the flow happens
The pulsations are ultimately driven by the cerebral circulation. Arterial blood arrives through the carotid and basilar arteries and is distributed by the anterior, middle, and posterior cerebral arteries; venous blood drains through the superior sagittal and transverse sinuses (Figure 4). Directly imaging the vascular pulsation over a single heartbeat shows the negative MR signal changes propagating through the vasculature ((vid-brainbeats-vasculature?)).






Figure 4: Blood flow schematic: arterial supply (carotid/basilar, anterior/middle/ posterior cerebral arteries) and venous drainage (superior sagittal, transverse sinuses).





Video
Vasculature: negative MR pulsations over a single heartbeat.


The same cardiac cycle drives CSF motion. CSF flows from the lateral ventricles through the third and fourth ventricles and out into the subarachnoid spaces (Figure 5), and this pulsatile flow is increasingly thought to matter for clearance of metabolic waste from the brain.






Figure 5: CSF flow schematic: from the lateral and third ventricles through the fourth ventricle into the subarachnoid spaces.
crumbs: Brain Beats: Pulsatile Motion and Flow

title: Achieving Reproducibility: Perspectives and New Tools
text:
Motivation: a reproducibility problem with two different causes
Much of the public conversation about reproducibility in neuroscience and psychology focuses on statistical reproducibility — whether N is large enough, whether p is small enough, whether the right test was used, or, in the worst cases, outright research misconduct (fabricated or manipulated images have been the basis of several recent high-profile retractions and investigations, as documented in books such as Bad Blood by John Carreyrou and Rigor Mortis by Richard Harris). But for a center that manages MRI data for many labs, a different and more tractable problem is at least as important: computational reproducibility — whether the specific chain of software, parameters, and data versions that produced a given result can be recovered and rerun at all, independent of whether the underlying statistics were sound. Replication (repeating an experiment to see if the scientific finding holds up) and computational reproducibility (recovering the exact computational pipeline behind a result) are related but distinct goals, and an MRI center is much better positioned to guarantee the second than the first, since replicating expensive, complex MRI experiments is not something a data-management platform can solve on its own.
Computational reproducibility is not something that can be bolted on after the fact. It has to be designed into a project from the beginning, with a set of programming and research disciplines that are maintained throughout the project’s life. Large, well-funded projects like the Human Connectome Project (HCP) and the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study have this discipline built in — but the argument here is that every lab should have access to it, not just the largest consortia.
crumbs: Achieving Reproducibility: Perspectives and New Tools

title: Achieving Reproducibility: Perspectives and New Tools
section: From simple beginnings to a data-management problem
text:
From simple beginnings to a data-management problem
In the early 1990s, MRI acquisition was comparatively simple, and there was correspondingly little need — or ability — to do much in the way of data management; computational infrastructure and data-analysis methods were primitive by later standards (Figure 2). By the time a new MRI center for cognitive and neurobiological imaging was being built roughly fifteen years later, in 2008, both the instrumentation and the computational demands had grown substantially more complex, and Stanford’s own IT infrastructure could not, by itself, solve the data-management problem that running a modern multi-user MRI center creates (Figure 3).






Figure 2: MRI acquisition in 1992: simpler hardware, and correspondingly limited computational infrastructure for data management.









Figure 3: Building the Stanford Center for Cognitive and Neurobiological Imaging (CNI) in 2008 raised data-management questions that the scanner hardware alone could not answer.
crumbs: Achieving Reproducibility: Perspectives and New Tools

title: Achieving Reproducibility: Perspectives and New Tools
section: Data management as a prerequisite to computational reproducibility
text:
Data management as a prerequisite to computational reproducibility
The starting point is architectural: data should be archived at the center itself, before it ever leaves, and made available through a platform-independent web browser rather than requiring users to re-gather or manually copy their own data for each analysis or publication (Figure 4). Storing data thoughtfully at the point of capture — rather than simply handing raw files out to whoever asks — is treated here as close to a professional obligation, not a nicety.






Figure 4: Archiving data at the center and exposing it through a platform-independent web browser removes the burden on individual users to re-gather data for publication or re-analysis.



Underneath that browser-based access sits a data capture architecture that has to classify and interpret many different kinds of MR data — raw DICOM from the instrument or a hospital PACS system, legacy data users want to add retroactively, behavioral and physiological recordings that matter for reproducibility, and the output of custom reconstruction pipelines — and route all of it, de-identified, into a per-project store (Figure 5).






Figure 5: The Flywheel data capture architecture: a reaper process classifies, de-identifies, and uploads many different MR and non-MR data types into a user’s project.
crumbs: Achieving Reproducibility: Perspectives and New Tools

title: Achieving Reproducibility: Perspectives and New Tools
text:
Tools are better than rules
A recurring lesson from running a multi-user center: it works better to give users good tools than to try to enforce data-management rules by policy alone. Users have different preferences for how they want to pre-process their data, project membership changes over time so permissions need to be easy to manage, and many users want help with pre-processing, project notes, and visualization rather than being left to solve those problems themselves (Figure 6).






Figure 6: Tools, not just rules: gear rules, per-user permissions, and a built-in image viewer, all attached directly to a project.



In practice, this means packaging common computations as installable, shareable units — called Gears in Flywheel — so that many kinds of analysis can be installed once and shared between users. A single lab’s site might share dozens of Gears with collaborators, including FreeSurfer, FSL, HCP pipelines, tractography tools, file-format converters (DICOM), and directory-structure converters (BIDS), among others (Figure 7). Every time a Gear runs, its parameters are stored automatically in the project’s provenance record, so that exactly how a given result — a FreeSurfer run, for example — was produced can always be recovered later (Figure 8).






Figure 7: Gears package common analyses (FreeSurfer, FSL, HCP pipelines, tractography, format conversion, and more) as installable, shareable units.









Figure 8: Computational record keeping: the Gears used and their parameters are stored automatically in a project’s Provenance tab.
crumbs: Achieving Reproducibility: Perspectives and New Tools

title: Achieving Reproducibility: Perspectives and New Tools
text:
Cloud-scale computing and programmatic access
“Cloud-scale” here means something specific: the ability to select and run many Gears across many different data sets at the same time, with the cloud provider handling the underlying machine provisioning on demand (Figure 9). This matters because data sets have grown larger and analyses more complex — capacity that would be impractical for an individual lab to provision and maintain on its own.






Figure 9: Cloud-scale computing: many Gears can be run across many data sets simultaneously, with compute capacity provisioned on demand.



Beyond pre-packaged Gears, programmers need to be able to write their own special-purpose scripts and explore new methods. A software development kit (SDK) exposes language bindings for Python, MATLAB, and R, along with REST database endpoints, so that new computations can be developed and shared just as easily as the pre-packaged ones (Figure 10). In practice, this SDK can be driven from a Jupyter notebook or a MATLAB Live Script to search for data, download it, run an analysis such as a FreeSurfer segmentation, and upload the resulting analysis back into the system — a complete round trip from query to stored, reproducible result (Figure 11).






Figure 10: Language bindings (SDK) for Python, MATLAB, and R, plus REST database endpoints, support exploration and new methods development.









Figure 11: A MATLAB Live Script driving the SDK: search Flywheel for T1-weighted files, download them, run a FreeSurfer segmentation, and upload the analysis back to the project.

title: Achieving Reproducibility: Perspectives and New Tools
text:
Databases built for different purposes
At the time of publication, curated data is often placed on a shared public site such as OpenNeuro, the NIMH Data Archive (NDA), the USC Laboratory of Neuro Imaging’s Image and Data Archive (IDA), or FITBIR, among others (LORIS, COINS, and XNAT serve similar roles). These sites add real value — checking data quality and providing standard pipelines — but they are designed for a different purpose than an MRI center’s own data system: they are built to host curated, published data for reuse, not to manage an ongoing project’s full range of cloud computation (Figure 12).






Figure 12: Public data-sharing platforms (OpenNeuro, NDA, IDA, FITBIR) serve a different purpose than a center’s own data-management system.



Statistical reproducibility is a related but separate concern from the computational reproducibility this resource focuses on. Null-hypothesis statistical testing and group comparisons remain deeply embedded in neuroscience’s publication culture, particularly in cognitive and clinical neuroscience, and the NIH itself has published principles and guidelines for reporting rigorous, reproducible preclinical research (National Institutes of Health (n.d.)). The tools described here are built to support many kinds of computation — not to adjudicate the final statistical hypothesis test.
crumbs: Achieving Reproducibility: Perspectives and New Tools

title: Achieving Reproducibility: Perspectives and New Tools
text:
FAIR principles
Flywheel’s design is explicitly an attempt to implement the FAIR principles — a set of community-developed guidelines stating that data (or any digital object) should be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (Wilkinson et al. (2016)). Computational reproducibility, in this framing, is what it looks like to take the FAIR principles seriously in the specific context of a working MRI center: measure quantitatively, build computational models on top of those measurements, and build the whole pipeline so that it can be checked and shared (Figure 13).






Figure 13: The FAIR Guiding Principles for scientific data management and stewardship (Wilkinson et al. (2016)), the framework Flywheel is built to implement.

We begin with an overview of the MRI instrumentation. An MRI system is organized across multiple rooms: the scanner room containing the magnet bore, the console room for the operator, and the machine room containing the gradient amplifiers and support electronics. We describe how superconducting magnets generate the main magnetic field (\(B_0\)) and introduce the standard units of magnetic field strength.
Next, we introduce the two main types of electromagnetic coils:

Radiofrequency (RF) coils, which excite nuclear spins and record the resulting signals. We explore this process at the beginning of the next part, starting with the free induction decay experiment in Introduction to MR signals.
Gradient coils, which vary the magnetic field spatially to enable image formation.

Finally, we discuss MRI safety, outlining the physical hazards of working around a high-field magnet and the essential safety practices required for all operators and subjects.

title: MR Signals
text:
Work in Progress



Suggestions of all kinds for these lecture notes are welcome — whether it’s fixing small errors, raising bigger questions, or offering new perspectives. Please share comments through GitHub Issues. This part of the course develops the physical model behind every MR measurement, starting from a single voltage recorded from a beaker of water and ending with the pulse sequences used to control what that voltage reflects.
We begin with the free induction decay (FID): apply a radiofrequency pulse to a sample sitting in the main field, and the coil that produced the pulse detects a voltage that oscillates and decays. The next chapter develops the macroscopic model that explains this experiment — the main field, \(B_0\), creates an equilibrium magnetization; the RF field, \(B_1\), tips it away from equilibrium by an amount set by the flip angle; the resulting transverse magnetization precesses and induces the measured voltage; and relaxation returns the magnetization toward equilibrium, by two physically distinct routes.
Those two routes are \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) relaxation, each given its own chapter. \(T_1\) (spin-lattice) relaxation describes how the longitudinal component recovers, at a rate set by how efficiently a spin’s excess energy transfers to its molecular surroundings; \(T_2\) (spin-spin) relaxation describes how the transverse component decays as individual spins lose their common phase, separating further into an irreversible spin-spin contribution and a reversible field-inhomogeneity contribution that together produce the faster-decaying \(T_2^*\). \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) are two of the three basic sources of MR image contrast, and these chapters show how their different tissue values make gray matter, white matter, and CSF appear bright or dark depending on which relaxation process an image is weighted toward.
The following two chapters turn these relaxation mechanisms into working pulse sequences. Spin echo uses a second, 180° RF pulse to reverse the reversible dephasing and recover a signal — the Hahn echo — well after the FID itself has vanished, making it possible to measure the pure \(T_2\) decay directly. Inversion recovery instead inverts the longitudinal magnetization outright and reads it out after a chosen delay; it is the reference method for measuring \(T_1\), and, through its FLAIR variant, a way to null a chosen tissue — typically CSF — directly in a clinical image.
The part closes with a review chapter that consolidates the instrumentation, the macroscopic model, and the \(T_1\)/\(T_2\)/spin-echo/inversion-recovery material into a single reference summary, before the book turns, in the next part, to how these single-voxel measurements are extended into images.

title: Visual Neuroscience with fMRI
text:
Work in Progress



Suggestions of all kinds for these lecture notes are welcome — whether it’s fixing small errors, raising bigger questions, or offering new perspectives. Please share comments through GitHub Issues. This part of the course is about visual neuroscience, mainly as studied using fMRI. The organizing question throughout is how the visual field comes to be represented in cortex — not once, but many times over — and what the cortex does with those representations once they exist.
We begin with the evidence that vision is a construction rather than a direct readout of the world: illusions such as Shepard’s “Turning the Tables,” Lotto and Purves’s lightness displays, and the rotating hollow-mask face show that perception can diverge sharply from the physical stimulus, reflecting an inference the visual system draws from context rather than a transparent measurement of it.
Having established that cortex constructs a representation, the next chapter asks a more basic, historical question: whether a “visual cortex” exists at all, and where. The answer runs through a 19th-century priority dispute between Ferrier and Munk, confirmation in human patients by Henschen, and the first systematic maps of the visual field onto V1, drawn independently by Inouye and Holmes from soldiers’ gunshot wounds in the Russo-Japanese and First World Wars. The chapter closes by tracing the subcortical route the signal takes to get there — the optic chiasm, the layered lateral geniculate nucleus, and the disproportionate expansion of cortex relative to its thalamic input.
V1 turned out to be only the first of many such maps. The following chapter follows the discovery of additional maps, beginning with electrode recordings in rabbit and cat, extending — laboriously — into primate, and arriving finally at fMRI, whose spatial resolution made it practical to measure a dozen or more human visual field maps directly, using traveling-wave stimuli that sweep systematically through eccentricity and polar angle.
With a whole catalog of maps in hand, the next chapter turns to how they relate to one another, working through three organizing principles in turn: two large processing streams for object and spatial vision, a graded hierarchy of feedforward and feedback connections, and clusters of neighboring maps that share a common eccentricity representation.
The part closes by asking whether cortex is organized by more than retinotopy alone — whether some regions are specialized for particular categories of visual content. Reading provides the historical test case, from 19th-century connectionist accounts of alexia through Kanwisher’s fMRI localization of the fusiform face area and related category-selective regions for places, words, and body parts, which sit alongside, and in places overlap, the retinotopic maps described earlier.
